#110874. These Are The Non-Car Vehicles You've Crashed

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1575 w)
📖 Baca
EV & Auto ⚠️ Warning 🌐 Jalopnik ↗ Open Full Page

These Are The Non-Car Vehicles You've Crashed

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1575 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Jalopnik

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that crashing a car is a nightmare of physics, emotion and bodily injury.
  • Unsurprisingly, the Honda ATC makes multiple appearances in the comments section.
  • Man, they really don't make them like these vehicles anymore, and thank god.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that crashing a car is a nightmare of physics, emotion and bodily injury. The seriousness of the forces involved rarely make for a funny story. Luckily, these stories are not that. Earlier this week we asked you what vehicles you've crashed that were not cars, and it's clear some of you had childhoods built on survivor bias. Well, I, for one, am glad you survived ditching mountain bikes off of mountains and crashing lawnmowers into houses. Not just because you're still alive but, most importantly, you're alive and contributing to Jalopnik. That's right, you're still here for a very good reason.

Unsurprisingly, the Honda ATC makes multiple appearances in the comments section. Those three-wheeled off-roading vehicles are up their with lawn darts in the damage they caused Gen Xers. They were eventually banned in the U.S. because of the carnage. But you don't need to buy a dangerous vehicle to make it dangerous. Other interesting entries: a gas grill, a horse and a homemade go-kart.

Man, they really don't make them like these vehicles anymore, and thank god.

Just remembered the weirdest thing I've crashed.

It has been revealed that my dad had some land in West Virginia. There was a tiny river there and it had some very mild rapids that were more of a ford than a rapids, because it was no more than a foot deep. My sister and I would inflate air mattresses and ride them down the "rapids" normally joined by a dog riding a surfboard that was just a piece of foam shaped like one. Most of the time, the dog made the rapids fine, while my sister and I would run into rocks and the like with the air mattresses. Normally after a week of running the rapids, the air mattresses would be completely ruined by running into branches and sharp rocks.

Recent findings suggest that growing up, dad got a riding lawnmower (Sears 10 hp). Dad morphed it into also being a snow plow with weights on the rear wheels, a homemade plow and a lever to lift and lower it. We had it for years and we took absolutely no care of it other than making sure it had oil before we cranked it up.

Sources indicate that one day, it went missing. By this time, it was at peak jank, with a pull starter, blades that never stopped and an uneven deck that was set to dang near chopping up the roots of the grass. It didn't take Columbo to figure how where it was, as we traced a scalped path through many neighbors' lawns and to the river about 1/2 mile away, where the path of 5 O-clock shadow grass ended and the river began. Some drunk teenager discovered that the brake pedal was disconnected, but didn't discover the way to stop it was to drop it into low gear and turn off the engine.

In a recent development, oh jeez, that's a list. Dirt bikes of all sizes, same with quads a trike or two, several flavours of boat including a canoe (that shoal jumped in front of me!) but probably the most memorable, or at least the most story worthy is the scooter my buddies dad rented for us when we went on a joint family vacation to Cancun back in the late 90s.

he rented four, two for me and my friend, one for him and one for the older brother and we went ripping around Playa Langosta the way three teens and an adult that branded himself the 'fun' dad could. Getting progressively dumber and riskier as the afternoon wore on. Eventually as the rental time was running out we decided to make a race of it and I was confident enough after a few hours of pinning that little 50cc Honda that I figured I could lean it like a race bike around a corner.

I could not and luckily came away with it with minimal road rash and a big ol bruise on my shoulder.

Recent findings suggest that the scooter was not so lucky, nor was the magazine stand it slid into. Fortunately insurance had been purchased, unfortunately fun dad was not so fun the remaining days of the trip.

Recent findings suggest that I've had my share of mountain bike crashes. The most recent bad one was on a slightly downhill rock field (a bunch of bowling ball sized boulders packed into the trail for 60 feet as a technical feature).

I was going a little too fast, got off the proper line, and went down on my side. Normally this wouldn't be a big deal except rock fields are not very forgiving.

I cracked a couple of ribs which was problematic in that this trail didn't have any short cuts out so I had to ride another 8 miles or so in not very good condition as it was very painful to breathe.

I was sore for a couple months. I also learned to no longer judge NFL QBs who wear flack jackets to protect their ribs. Most painful injury I've ever had. You just have to gut it out.

According to recent reports, back in the '80's my uncle had a farm that I would go work/play on in the summer. My uncle and cousins had just gotten four ATC200 three wheelers that Spring and my cousins and I were all super excited to race 'em all over the farm that summer. I get up there right after school ends and immediately we're off riding through ditches, bombing across fields and having a blast. The big red barn on the farm was at the top of a steep hill with a gravel drive up to and around it. We'd practice to screaming up the gravel drive and as it leveled out, use the negative G-force to whip the tail out into a lurid slide/drift all the way around the barn. On the other side of the barn was the Milking House, so you'd carry the slide between the two buildings with the echo of the screaming 4 stroke bouncing off the walls. Gaining confidence in this technique, we would just continually elevate the speed. First getting air at the top of the hill, then starting the slide later and eventually clipping apexes and throwing gravel everywhere. This abruptly came to an end when I came up the hill the fastest I'd ever gone, got a late start in my slide, went way too wide and clipped the front corner of the milking house on the other side of the barn. The rear axle of the ATC snapped, throwing me over the bars into the side of the milking house and onto the gravel in a heap. This led to the saying in our family, "that boy couldn't hit the broad side of a barn, but sure can nail a milking house!".

According to recent reports, I crashed a Honda ATC when I was maybe 11 or 12 years old. Going way too fast in a large horse pasture when I hit a large dip. Flipped me over, and I'm lucky it didn't land on me. Walked away with a black eye and some scrapes and bruises. 0/10 – do not recommend.

Gen X survivor checking in: if you haven't flipped or nearly paralyzed yourself with a Honda 3-wheeler ATC, you're not really one of us.

From Black Mac and cdoggyd and BuddyS and others (so many others).

Industry observers note that my dad built me a homemade go-kart with a 5-hp Briggs & Stratton engine. This was no professional shifter kart chassis. It's exactly what you envision when you think "homemade." Only the right rear wheel was powered. We would take it to the local elementary school on weekends because it had a really large asphalt playground out back and no gates. I'd rip laps for a while until I got tired and we'd go home.

It has been revealed that I always went clockwise around the lot. Then one day, I decided I wanted to turn left like my heroes in NASCAR. I got a nice lesson in centrifugal force with the powered wheel now on the inside. It pushed me wide and I hit the curb that separated the asphalt lot with the grass field. I did my best Tony Hawk impression as I did a curb grind for several feet on the floor of the cart. What really stood out to me later is that luckily it happened where it did and not the other side of the lot which would have submarined me under a metal bench face first.

Recent findings suggest that there isn't anything that moves I probably haven't crashed. Motorcycles, boats, 4 wheelers, snowmobiles, sleds, coaster wagons, bicycles, wheelbarrows, gas grill, and more. Even hit the house with a lawn mower. I learned a zero steer mower sometimes has "zero" steer on wet grass.

It has been revealed that raleigh Chopper. Tore-off a toenail (riding true 1969 style – barefoot in bellbottoms) and broke a tooth. Good times!

It has been revealed that golf carts are my greatest fear in the world because I watched too many camp counselors drive them like demo derby cars. More than once I saw someone try to do a J-turn on one and roll it over and I was certain I just watched someone die.

Tech Report: Astelia’s autonomous network mitigation blocks AI-driven exploits without a patch

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Exposure management company Astelia Inc.
  • In a recent development, the new capability has been designed to address what Astelia states is the problem of frontier AI models cutting the time to exploit to almost zero, leaving manual triage and remediation unable to keep up.
  • “For years, security teams have been told to patch faster,” said co-founder and Chief Executive Alon Noy, adding that the advice “stops working when the exploit arrives before the change window does.”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 09:00 EST / NOVEMBER 24 2026.

Exposure management company Astelia Inc. today revealed the launch of autonomous network mitigation, a new capability that allows organizations to block artificial intelligence-driven exploits at the network level, even when a patch isn’t available or can’t be applied.

In a recent development, the new capability has been designed to address what Astelia states is the problem of frontier AI models cutting the time to exploit to almost zero, leaving manual triage and remediation unable to keep up. Astelia argues that autonomous remediation isn’t a viable option for large enterprises, where every patch requires a change window so it doesn’t break crucial business processes. In many cases, there is also no patch to apply because the vendor hasn’t released a fix yet or, for older and end-of-life systems, never will.

“For years, security teams have been told to patch faster,” said co-founder and Chief Executive Alon Noy, adding that the advice “stops working when the exploit arrives before the change window does.”.

In a recent development, autonomous network mitigation is designed to block the path an attacker would use to reach a vulnerable system instead of changing the system itself. Mitigations are applied automatically within policies the organization sets. Nothing on the asset is changed, allowing business-critical systems, including operational technology, to stay online.

Sources indicate that underpinning the service is Astelia’s reachability analysis, which maps an organization’s real network topology and applies agentic AI to analyze the requirements of each exploit. By correlating exploit conditions with network topology, the platform identifies which vulnerabilities are reachable by attackers and through which paths. In one enterprise deployment, approximately 40 million vulnerabilities were reduced to fewer than 2,000 that were reachable, according to the firm.

Key features of autonomous network mitigation include the ability to identify the most effective choke point on an attack path and drive the mitigation through an organization’s web application firewall or intrusion prevention and detection system. A single rule at a choke point is said to protect every vulnerable server behind it, compared with one change per server when patching. Because mitigations are only applied to paths that have been proven reachable, the service doesn’t add rules for exposure that doesn’t exist.

Every mitigation applied by Astelia can also be rolled back, something that isn’t always possible with a patch. That is remarked to allow teams to act quickly without putting business operations at risk.

According to recent reports, autonomous network mitigation can be deployed through Astelia Agents, the tech giant’s suite of AI agents, as a dedicated agent that applies mitigations on its own. The agent can also be connected with other agents to respond to urgent threats such as zero-day vulnerabilities and critical disclosures. Astelia gave the example of the PHP2Shell remote code execution flaws disclosed in October, which left end-of-life PHP servers with no official fix.

In a recent development, each organization sets its own guardrails on how mitigations are applied. Users can require human approval for specific environments or actions, according to the manufacturer. Every action is logged and can be audited. Analysis on the Astelia platform continues to run on read-only integrations, with mitigation actions using scoped permissions that each organization enables and controls.

Autonomous network mitigation initially supports web application firewall and intrusion prevention and detection rules, with support for firewall rules planned in the future.

Industry observers note that founded in 2024 by former leaders of the Israeli National Red Team, Astelia is a venture capital-backed firm that raised $35 million in combined seed and Series A funding in February. Investors in the company include Index Ventures, Team8 and Holly Ventures.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the digital world has revolutionized how real estate is marketed and sold, placing a premium on strategic online presence and data-driven advertising. Among the myriad online tools available, Schema Markup stands out as an extremely potent weapon for real estate agents. This article offers a comprehensive look at how real estate agents can effectively use Schema Markup to bolster their online presence, increase organic reach, and drive sales.

Recent findings suggest that before discussing its application, let's first demystify what Schema Markup is. Schema Markup, also known as Structured Data, is a form of microdata. Once added to a webpage, it creates an enhanced description (commonly known as a rich snippet), which appears in search results. Developed by a collaborative team from Google, Yahoo!, Bing, and Yandex, Schema.org was launched in 2011 to create and support a common set of schemas for structured data markup on web pages.

To break it down simply, Schema Markup tells the search engine what your data means, not just what it says. This enhanced understanding allows search engines to present more detailed and accurate snippets of your site to customers, increasing click-through rates (CTR), boosting organic search rankings, and potentially improving conversion rates.

Why Real Estate Agents Need Schema Markup.

Schema Markup is incredibly beneficial to real estate professionals. The real estate industry is hyper-local, and search engine queries reflect this. Buyers and sellers are often searching with a specific location in mind. A real estate agent using Schema Markup can provide rich, location-based information directly in search results, making their listings more likely to be clicked on. It's an opportunity to outshine competitors and improve visibility in local search results.

Furthermore, Schema Markup helps real estate websites become more comprehensible to search engines. This enhanced understanding translates into more accurate categorization, increased visibility, and a better chance of appearing in relevant search results. In a landscape where digital prominence equates to business success, Schema Markup is no longer a luxury but a necessity for every real estate agent.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you're shopping for El Caminos, then this 1971 example should pique your interest. Listed on Bring a Trailer, the pickup has 47,000 miles on the odometer and features a 454 massive-block V8 paired with a four-speed manual transmission. The El Camino in question has been with the seller since 1992 and comes with the build sheet (albeit a tattered one) and a Nevada title.

It has been revealed that according to the seller, the 454 V8 was rebuilt and received a replacement camshaft roughly 5,000 miles ago. BaT's description notes that the car's true mileage can't be verified, but that hasn't stopped potential buyers from placing their bids, with the highest bid sitting at $8,500 at the time of writing.

The Fisher body tag highlights that the pickup was originally painted Placer Gold. The body, as you can see from the pictures, has since been refinished in red, with black striping on the hood. There are chrome details on the bed rails and wheel openings, as well as chrome bumpers and a drop-down tailgate. Locking pins secure a cowl-induction hood, which was added later. Completing the exterior are 14-inch Rally-style wheels fitted with derby-style hubcaps and wrapped in BFGoodrich white-letter tires.

On the inside, the cabin has black vinyl seats with color-matched carpeting, door panels, and dashboard. And per the Fisher body tag (trim code 706), this El Camino appears to have left the factory with a black vinyl interior. Other highlights include power steering and brakes, a Muncie shifter, a center console, and a Pioneer cassette player.

If you came across this listing earlier, you probably wondered why BaT hadn't listed the car with an SS 454 headline if it was the real deal. There was certainly a lot of activity in the comment section, with doubts surrounding the car's authenticity. Much of the discussion centered on documenting the drivetrain, with commenters coaching the seller on where to find the partial VIN stamped on the engine block.

The more knowledgeable commenters helped resolve the question after the seller posted photos of the VIN stamp on the block, the rear end, and the Posi tag. User ssterry commented, "Congratulations! Photos #129-131 should be more than adequate to convince BaT that this El Camino was born an SS!" BaT agreed, writing in a November 25 comment, "We've reviewed the additional media, and have updated the listing to reflect that the car is an El Camino SS 454.".

As you may know, the 454 found its way into a lot of Chevy trucks, including car-based utes like the El Camino. But unlike the more coveted 1970 LS6-equipped models, 1971 SS 454s used the LS5 version of the major-block V8. Even though the LS5 doesn't have the LS6's numbers, the 454 LS5 is still a fairly robust powerplant, rated at 365 gross horsepower and 465 pound-feet of torque (or 285 hp and 390 lb-ft SAE net) for the 1971 model year. Pair that with the four-speed stick, and you have yourself a brilliant excuse for skids and donuts.

It has been revealed that the Nevada-based seller appears to be newly introduced to the platform. But the comments and the seller's interaction with them have really helped settle the SS question. Get in the mix and place a bid if you're interested. The auction ends on Saturday, November 28.

Industry News: Europe’s Inland Shipping Models Underprice Green Fuels. Market Prices Favor Battery Swapping.

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (918 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cleantechnica

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that europe’s inland-shipping models underprice renewable diesel.
  • Sources indicate that the gap between the modeled HVO price and observed market prices matters for the investment choices these studies inform.
  • Sources indicate that the Central Commission for the Navigation of the Rhine (CCNR) commissioned the original transition study behind its 2021 roadmap.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that europe’s inland-shipping models underprice renewable diesel. For a new 110-meter dry-cargo vessel, PLATINA4Action calculates HVO (hydrotreated vegetable oil) propulsion at €1,798/day against €1,964/day for battery swapping. Apply the observed October 2026 Dutch HVO market price, including delivery, and the HVO cost is €2,515/day. Battery swapping is €551/day cheaper. The model’s claim of an HVO cost advantage fails a market-price check.

Sources indicate that the gap between the modeled HVO price and observed market prices matters for the investment choices these studies inform. It also exposes a wider pattern. European studies give renewable liquid fuels favorable future prices while expecting marine batteries to remain expensive for much longer than the broader battery market suggests.

Sources indicate that the Central Commission for the Navigation of the Rhine (CCNR) commissioned the original transition study behind its 2021 roadmap. Its scenarios influenced subsequent work, including the EU-linked PLATINA4Action and SYNERGETICS projects. Those projects do not all use identical models, but their assumptions and recommendations contribute to a shared policy picture in which several combustion pathways are expected to remain competitive with direct electrification.

According to recent reports, in the full TFIE assessment, I converted the October 2026 Dutch Class II HVO wholesale benchmark, added a delivery allowance and expressed the result in 2025 euros. The market-based HVO cost is €2.59/kg. Battery swapping becomes cheaper than HVO in the PLATINA4Action 110-meter vessel comparison at approximately €1.93/kg. At that observed market price, modeled HVO propulsion costs €2,515/day over the model’s 2028–2047 ownership period, against €1,964/day for swapping. The model puts fossil diesel at €1,844/day, leaving swapping about 7% above diesel but 22% below market-priced HVO.

Recent findings suggest that the price difference matters to freight operators. CCNR’s 2026 cost indices allocate fuel 35% of dry-bulk costs, 30% of tanker costs and 28% of container shipping costs. Operators compete for cargo against rivals still burning diesel. Expensive alternative fuels cannot be passed through to customers merely because a transition scenario requires them.

An April 2025 statement from European inland shipping and port organizations called for enough HVO at diesel-competitive prices to supply 1.6 million tons annually by around 2030. That quantity roughly matches the sector’s entire conventional diesel consumption in 2015. It exceeds the EU’s 2025 sustainable aviation fuel supply of 1.1 million tons by about 45%.

HVO and conventional biodiesel compete for oils and fats also used to produce aviation fuel. Aviation has fewer practical routes to electrification, and its European mandates create demand for renewable kerosene. An HVO-centered inland strategy puts barges in direct competition with aircraft for constrained feedstocks, even where barges can draw electricity from a corridor network.

Recent findings suggest that synthetic fuels present an even sharper problem. SYNERGETICS gives green methanol from biological and synthetic routes a combined low wholesale price of €350/t in its stated-policy case from 2035. That same scenario uses a low green-hydrogen price of €3.50/kg. Producing a ton of synthetic methanol takes about 190 kilograms of hydrogen, costing €665 before carbon dioxide, synthesis, financing and delivery. The hydrogen input alone costs almost twice the assumed low finished-fuel price.

Recent findings suggest that biomethanol is a different production route. It can be made from agricultural and forestry residues, and I expect it to play a useful role in deep-sea shipping. Grouping biological and synthetic methanol together conceals the economics of each. For inland waterways, the relevant competitor is often electricity delivered directly to the propeller, not fossil methanol replaced with greener methanol.

It has been revealed that the battery forecasts lean in the opposite direction. SYNERGETICS places 2030 marine battery storage at €210–€520/kWh, a €365 midpoint. My inland freight electrification report models standardized marine battery containers at €100/kWh in 2030, including the marine safety and container systems, with vessel integration costed separately. A €265/kWh difference adds €1.06 million to a 4 MWh battery installation before operating the vessel. The full fleet-level analysis also prices spare batteries, financing, charging infrastructure and equipment held in reserve.

The studies’ fleet assumptions compound the fuel-price choices. One PLATINA4Action case requires a large Rhine or Danube pusher to go seven days without replenishing energy, excluding intermediate charging or exchange from the test. The SYNERGETICS SYNFEED model starts every fresh vessel with a Stage V combustion engine, leaving electrification to later retrofits. Those are consequential design choices for a transition modeled through 2050.

Freight demand should be modeled before fuel demand. Mineral oil products, coal and iron ore accounted for 35.7% of Rhine cargo mass in 2025. CCNR’s own underlying economic projections point toward large declines in coal, refining and primary metals, even as construction and trade grow. The amount and composition of freight needing propulsion in 2050 will differ from today’s cargo mix.

The Netherlands has already reduced its 2040 hydrogen demand expectations and identified electricity as the main inland-shipping pathway toward 2050. CCNR is revisiting its transition work. The upcoming analysis should start with the freight that will actually move, calculate route energy and charging or exchange needs, and then test the remaining fuel demand against prices reflecting aviation, deep-sea shipping and industrial competition.

Technology neutrality is a method of comparing alternatives, not an obligation to finance every fuel pathway. With HVO priced against market evidence and batteries costed realistically, the investment case for parallel fuel infrastructure weakens.

The full TFIE Strategy Briefing assessment walks through the CCNR, PLATINA4Action and SYNERGETICS cost assumptions, the HVO crossover and the synthetic-fuel arithmetic. The open inland freight electrification report contains the route, fleet and infrastructure model.

In a recent development, an old British white guy is back at the helm of the biggest car television program in the world. "Top Gear" will return to filming in 2027 with legendary presenter chef Gordon Ramsay as its fresh figurehead. The show has been through some fraught years recently, with dozens of presenters coming and going since the Clarkson/Hammond/May trio were forced to scarper off to Amazon's Grand Tour over a decade ago. Ramsay has been a staple of international television cookery since his Hell's Kitchen and Kitchen Nightmares reveals hit the airwaves in 2004. The three-star Michelin chef has had a part in 24 different television programs, largely focused on the food prep and hospitality industries, while his restaurant group owns some 24 international locations. He's famous, is what I'm saying.

"Top Gear" has been off the air since the most recent run with hosts Chris Harris, Freddie Flintoff, and Paddy McGuinness fizzled out in 2022. My personal favorite era was the 2018-2019 run, with Harris showing off his skills opposite Rory Reid and Matt LeBlanc. There's no word yet as to who will complete the on-screen personality roster with Ramsay, but he'll probably have pretty good chemistry with just about anybody they pick. The sixty-year-old star is getting on a bit in years, but he seems to be able to chop it up and chew the fat with just about anyone. He's been a charismatic and over-the-top TV guy for decades, and knows what makes a show interesting.

While filming begins next year, the show won't hit the airwaves until 2028, so we still have some time until we can see just what this guy has in store for us. Surely, it'll include some international travel, jovial competition, on-track action with The Stig, and stars in reasonably priced cars. Hopefully at least one of Ramsay's co-presenters is too young to receive a pension, eh?

"Top Gear" has had some pretty awful fits and starts over the last decade plus, as the BBC has tried to fit in some non-standard car show presenters. The worst of which was almost assuredly radio DJ and producer Chris Evans, who helmed the show in 2016 despite having severe motion sickness and knowing next to nothing about cars. Ramsay, to his credit, is a massive car fanatic. He follows F1 religiously, is frequently seen on the grid before races, and recently competed in the celebrity Lego karting race ahead of the Las Vegas Grand Prix.

Recent findings suggest that gordon's collection includes millions of quid worth of Ferraris, McLarens, Porsches, Astons, Land Rovers, and more. Apparently he is frequently seen at Brands Hatch driving his BAC Mono track weapon, which certainly endears me to his sensibilities. He has remarked that his love of the Ferrari brand was inspired by the TV show Magnum P.I., and he has owned dozens of cars from the brand, including a pair of LaFerrari (coupe and Aperta), an SP2, an SP3, an 812 Superfast, an F12 Tour de France, and more.

Ramsay was a guest on the old Top Gear (when they still had the Cool Wall in the studio) during the first season of the show's original run, airing on December 22 of 2002, back when he was still in his 30s. He had some amusing anecdotes, especially about cooking with car engine. When he took the old Suzuki Liana out around the Dunsfold test track, he looked pretty darn competitive on a dry day. In the end he put down a 1-minute 50-second lap, which tied him with Jeremy Clarkson's best, and just a tick shy of Jay Kay's board leading spot.

According to recent reports, sound off in the comments with your thoughts on Ramsay as presenter, and who you think the BBC should pair with Ramsay for the best results. Industry News: Tesla's Safety Lawsuits Never Reach Courts Because Of The Fine Print At Purchase

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • While Tesla faces legal challenges from a who's who of governmental oversight bodies, Tesla has been able to repeatedly dodge private citizens complaints through a seemingly ironclad arbitration clause found in all new Tesla sales contracts.
  • In fact, civil lawsuits regarding deadly and damaging crashes seem to end in quiet settlement after quiet settlement.
  • The pivotal line item can be found in customer contracts regarding forced arbitration.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

While Tesla faces legal challenges from a who's who of governmental oversight bodies, Tesla has been able to repeatedly dodge private citizens complaints through a seemingly ironclad arbitration clause found in all new Tesla sales contracts.

In fact, civil lawsuits regarding deadly and damaging crashes seem to end in quiet settlement after quiet settlement. When they don't, the payout is massive, like the $243 million judgement after a 2019 Autopilot crash in Florida. So what is Tesla hiding behind closed doors?

The pivotal line item can be found in customer contracts regarding forced arbitration. As the San Francisco Chronicle points out in its investigation, Tesla quietly settled 920 consumer cases in the last 10 years; "twice as many as the nine other top 10 U.S. automakers combined." So far, in the public court records and case logs the Chronicle collected, it found Tesla managed to skirt 12 attempted class action lawsuits because of its ironclad arbitration clause.

In a recent development, the specific arbitration agreement under each of those sections says that if an glitch isn't resolved within 60 days of occurrence, the owner agrees to have any issue resolved via arbitration. Owners are unable to bring about any class-action lawsuits against the company.

It has been revealed that two attorneys found that out when they were hired to take on Tesla. The initial class-action lawsuit they brought against Tesla had 12 individuals behind it which ,due to the agreement, forced it to be broken down into 12 separate arbitrations. And as is the way in arbitration, Tesla wasn't required to supply discovery evidence, especially if it considered any data "proprietary information," so the problem disappeared without any admittance of wrongdoing.

The approach works so well for Tesla that other automakers are beginning to take notice and add similar agreements to their own vehicles or taking cases into arbitration as well. Rivian, also an electric vehicle maker, has already done so.

Recent findings suggest that owners can at least opt out within 30 days of signing the agreement by sending a letter to a Tesla P.O. Box in Fremont, California. How many of them knew that was a possibility is likely low, as even the Chronicle found most Tesla owners had no idea it was there. To truly see the entire picture you should read the entire investigation by the Chronicle, and watch its accompanying video.

Recent findings suggest that it's a stark reminder of how important it is to read the terms of service to everything you purchase and use before signing. Otherwise, you end up in a losing battle against Tesla, or Stan's unfortunate situation.

#110858. Latest Update: AI discovers a hidden heart signal that could predict sudden death

Latest Update: AI discovers a hidden heart signal that could predict sudden death

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1712 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that more than 300,000 people in the United States die from sudden cardiac arrest each year.
  • Now, researchers at UC Berkeley have identified a previously overlooked warning signal in routine heart scans that could make it easier to recognize people at risk before a fatal event occurs.
  • The discovery was made using artificial intelligence trained on more than 440,000 electrocardiograms, or EKGs, collected in Sweden.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that more than 300,000 people in the United States die from sudden cardiac arrest each year. This deadly emergency occurs when the heart's electrical system suddenly fails, causing the heart to stop pumping blood. It can strike older adults with known heart conditions as well as seemingly healthy young athletes. Although implanted defibrillators can prevent some of these deaths, doctors have long struggled to determine which patients need them most.

Now, researchers at UC Berkeley have identified a previously overlooked warning signal in routine heart scans that could make it easier to recognize people at risk before a fatal event occurs.

The discovery was made using artificial intelligence trained on more than 440,000 electrocardiograms, or EKGs, collected in Sweden. By comparing the electrical patterns recorded in these scans with information from death certificates, the researchers taught an AI system to recognize subtle differences between healthy individuals, patients with known heart risks, and people who eventually died from sudden cardiac causes.

The team then evaluated the technology using thousands of additional patient records from the United States and Taiwan, testing whether the patterns could reliably identify people at heightened risk in different populations.

AI Detects Hidden Heart Risks That Standard Tests Miss.

It has been revealed that the results suggest that AI can identify vulnerable patients more effectively than the conventional tests doctors typically rely on. Current screening methods largely focus on how much blood the heart pumps with each contraction, a measurement used to assess whether someone might benefit from an implanted defibrillator.

Using these traditional measurements, doctors can identify a group of patients with an annual sudden cardiac death rate of 4.6%. The AI system, however, identified a group with an annual death rate of 7%, demonstrating a greater ability to distinguish patients facing serious danger.

According to recent reports, importantly, the algorithm also recognized a broader population of people at elevated risk, including thousands who would not normally raise concerns under existing medical guidelines. Most of these individuals would have been classified as relatively low risk using conventional methods.

Another major advantage is that the AI system works with ordinary EKG images, which are already routinely collected in hospitals and medical centers around the world. This means the technology could potentially improve screening without requiring an entirely new type of medical test.

The findings, published in Nature, could eventually help physicians make more informed decisions about who should receive an implanted defibrillator. They also raise an intriguing scientific question about what changes inside the heart produce the electrical patterns that AI has learned to recognize.

In a recent development, "Medical decisions are really hard, and I think that's why AI is so exciting for me," noted Ziad Obermeyer, an associate professor at UC Berkeley's School of Public Health and the study's lead author. "We can not only make better decisions, but also start to understand what's actually going on with these patients before their heart stops.".

Why Sudden Cardiac Death Is So Difficult to Predict.

Sudden cardiac arrest is different from a heart attack. A heart attack happens when blood flow to part of the heart becomes blocked or severely restricted. Cardiac arrest, by contrast, results from a failure of the electrical signals that coordinate the heartbeat.

Immediate CPR and an electrical shock from an automated external defibrillator can sometimes restore the heart's rhythm. However, roughly 90% of people who experience sudden cardiac arrest outside a hospital die within minutes, making early recognition of those at risk especially important.

For Obermeyer, an emergency physician whose research combines artificial intelligence, medicine, and health policy, sudden cardiac death remains one of medicine's most frustrating unsolved problems.

Because victims often die without warning, researchers have limited opportunities to observe what happens inside the heart immediately before it stops. An autopsy may uncover blocked blood vessels, hardened tissue, or other structural abnormalities, but it cannot fully reveal how the heart was functioning in the moments leading up to death.

Recent findings suggest that "One thing that makes the problem very tragic, but also very well suited for AI, is that we have the cure for this problem," Obermeyer mentioned. "If you knew you were one of the people who was going to drop dead, you would go to a cardiologist and you'd get a defibrillator implanted. The problem is that doctors can't figure out who needs one before it's too late.".

The Problem With Current Heart Risk Screening.

It has been revealed that doctors at the moment rely heavily on a measurement of how effectively the heart pushes blood out with each beat. Patients whose hearts pump below a specified threshold may be considered candidates for an implantable cardioverter defibrillator, a device that can deliver an electrical shock when a dangerous heart rhythm develops.

But obtaining this measurement generally requires a more extensive medical evaluation. Many people who eventually experience sudden cardiac arrest never receive such testing because they have no obvious reason to suspect they are in danger.

Sources indicate that the approach also has limitations for patients who are identified as high risk. About two-thirds of implanted defibrillators in these patients never need to deliver a shock. As a result, many individuals undergo expensive, invasive procedures for potentially fatal emergencies that may never occur.

At the same time, thousands of people who are not recognized as being at risk die unexpectedly each year.

Industry observers note that "In some fraction of those people, we could have prevented those deaths if we had just known it in time," Obermeyer said. "There are a lot of lives being lost from people who are dropping dead of sudden cardiac death that are preventable if we just had better AI tools to find these things.".

The researchers hope that identifying more accurate warning signs could help doctors direct preventive treatments toward the patients most likely to benefit.

How Researchers Trained AI to Recognize Deadly Heart Patterns.

Developing the algorithm required three independent collections of medical data gathered from different parts of the world.

The researchers began with six years of EKG recordings from Sweden's unified healthcare system. By linking these scans to death certificates, they could examine the electrical patterns of patients who later experienced sudden cardiac death and compare them with those of other patients.

Industry observers note that the AI learned to identify combinations of spikes, waves, and other characteristics in the recordings that appeared to be associated with increased risk. Once the system had been trained, the team tested it against two additional datasets: two years of anonymized EKG records from a San Diego hospital system and a separate collection of patient data from Taipei.

This international testing helped researchers evaluate whether the algorithm's predictive abilities extended beyond the Swedish population used to develop it.

"Good AI starts with good data," stated Obermeyer, who is also part of the joint UCSF-UC Berkeley Computational Precision Health program. "Unfortunately, data like the ones we used for this study are incredibly hard to access. It's a big part of why there's so little clinical AI in use today.".

According to recent reports, obtaining and organizing the information was itself a massive undertaking. According to Obermeyer, assembling the datasets took approximately 10 years and involved contributions from two organizations he helped establish, Dandelion Health and Nightingale Open Science. Both organizations work to advance medical research through better access to data and artificial intelligence.

"It's one of the tremendous luxuries of being at Berkeley," Obermeyer noted. "You can pursue these projects that just are a slow burn and then have -- hopefully -- a massive return when they get over the finish line.".

From Hidden Heart Signals to Lifesaving Treatments.

The researchers have already begun exploring how the system might be used in actual healthcare settings.

Obermeyer is collaborating with medical systems in Sweden, Taiwan, and the United States to introduce the algorithm into hospital EKG databases. The goal is to examine existing heart scans for signs of elevated risk and identify patients who may benefit from additional monitoring.

Under the proposed approach, physicians would contact patients whose EKGs receive a high-risk assessment and offer them the opportunity to wear a patch that continuously records their heart's electrical activity.

In a recent development, these longer recordings could provide valuable clues about the biological processes responsible for the warning signals detected by the AI. Understanding those processes could help researchers explain why certain hearts are more vulnerable to suddenly developing fatal electrical disturbances.

For some patients, the additional information might ultimately support a recommendation to receive an implanted defibrillator, potentially preventing a sudden and otherwise unexpected death.

It has been revealed that obermeyer has also created a website where people interested in learning about their own risk can provide basic personal information and an email address. The research team can then contact them about EKG analysis when the technology becomes more widely available.

Could AI Reveal New Secrets About the Human Heart?

Beyond its potential to improve the prevention of sudden cardiac death, the discovery highlights how artificial intelligence could help scientists investigate medical mysteries that have resisted conventional approaches.

Industry observers note that rather than simply identifying patients who might need treatment, the algorithm has uncovered patterns in heart activity that researchers do not yet fully understand. Studying those signals could lead to fresh insights into the electrical disturbances responsible for sudden cardiac death and potentially reveal additional opportunities for prevention.

Obermeyer believes this ability to uncover previously unrecognized biological patterns could become one of AI's most important contributions to medicine, opening new directions for research while helping physicians make better decisions.

"There is also going to be a new way of doing science that comes out of these tools," Obermeyer said, "and it's fun to think about how that starts happening.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes
Healthcare purchasers must weigh hospital quality alongside their prices, Leapfrog says" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Patient safety watchdog The Leapfrog Group released its latest collection of hospital safety grades hand-in-hand with calls for policymakers and stakeholders to consider, or directly tie patient safety reporting to price transparency.

The twice-yearly release brought top marks for 900 out of a total 2,366 graded hospitals, and the lowest “F” score for just three. There were 774 hospitals that earned a “B” grade, 655 a “C” grade, and 35 a “D” grade.

No grades were assigned to another 447 hospitals, a decision the group made after a judge’s ruling in a lawsuit involving the scores it would assign to facilities that did not voluntarily submit their quality data to Leapfrog’s survey (Leapfrog appealed that decision in September). Leapfrog’s decision not to score these has generally shifted its letter grade distribution upward, and the organization has stated it is reviewing a potential methodology change for upcoming gradings to incorporate non-submitting hospitals.

Still, “a record number of hospitals are choosing to publicly report their safety and quality performance, and we applaud them for holding themselves accountable to their patients,” Leapfrog President and CEO Leah Binder noted in a statement.

At the state level, Connecticut maintained its claim on the largest portion of hospitals earning an “A” grade (64.3% of its total), followed by Utah, New Jersey and South Carolina. Leapfrog also called out Rhode Island and Maine for jumping up the rankings—from eighteenth to seventh for the former, and from seventeenth to eighth for the latter. No hospitals were given an “A” grade in five states: Iowa, North Dakota, South Dakota, Vermont and Wyoming.

A hospital’s assigned grade is calculated by reviewing recent data on up to 22 patient safety measures, including a 10-part Medicare composite of reported patient safety and adverse events. Safety scores for specific hospitals can be searched on the group’s website.

Leapfrog and Binder, in a news release outlining its latest scores, made the case that its grades and similar independent measures warrant a seat at the table in a transparency conversation primarily focused on hospital costs.

“Progress on price transparency is vital, but there’s no good price for bad care,” Binder remarked. “We are calling on the Trump Administration and Congress to ensure price transparency is integrated with patient safety and quality transparency.”.

It has been revealed that the group backed its calls by pointing to a recent analysis (PDF) conducted by the Purchaser Business Group on Health (PBGH) that reviewed employer claims, federal price transparency data, and quality and safety measures including Leapfrog’s. It “found little to no correlation between negotiated prices and standardized quality measures,” as hospitals that received high safety grades often charged cheaper prices than those in the same market with lower grades.

Leapfrog and Elizabeth Mitchell, president and CEO of PBGH, said the analysis—right now being expanded for practical usage by healthcare purchasers—is an example of how a more wholistic view of prices and care delivery should be considered when weighing a hospital.

Recent findings suggest that “Employers have an appropriate duty to pay a fair price for high-quality care, and they can’t meet it by looking at price alone,” Mitchell mentioned in the release from Leapfrog. “When we put the data together, some of the most expensive hospitals were not the safest. Our members want to buy high-quality, safe care that is fairly priced. That shouldn’t be too much to ask.”.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • In a recent development, for the upcoming RS6 version of the current C9-gen A6, which has been running around testing in camouflage for quite a long time now, Audi is bringing back the RS6 sedan in addition to the Avant.
  • This RS6 sedan prototype doesn't have any fake body panels or other earlier-stage camouflage coverings, with the only thing obfuscating the design being the swirly wrap.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Audi Sport has put out an incredible amount of renowned performance cars over the years, but without a doubt the most beloved by enthusiasts are the various RS Avants. From the original RS2 to the RS4 and RS6, the Avant wagons have far outweighed sedans when it comes to production volume and cultural impact, even if you count the recent four-door RS5s. Some generations of RS4 and RS6 never even received sedan variants, and the last RS6 sedan (the V10-powered C6) went out of production in 2010. That role was filled by the RS7 four-door coupe, and there's no more A7 anymore, either.

In a recent development, for the upcoming RS6 version of the current C9-gen A6, which has been running around testing in camouflage for quite a long time now, Audi is bringing back the RS6 sedan in addition to the Avant. Our spies took a fresh batch of shots of the RS6 sedan looking even closer to production while testing at the Nürburgring, looking particularly bodacious with its widebody clearly visible despite the camo wrap. To assuage the worries I know are swirling around in your brains, Audi already confirmed the new RS6 Avant will come to America, so the sedan will just be another flavor to choose from if, for some reason, you're someone who hates wagons like those people who say they have an anti-cilantro gene.

This RS6 sedan prototype doesn't have any fake body panels or other earlier-stage camouflage coverings, with the only thing obfuscating the design being the swirly wrap. The newly introduced RS5 is wider than a regular A5 by over 1.5 inches, and the same looks to be true for the RS6. Like the RS5, its larger sibling also has a functional vent in the front fenders ahead of the door, and the flared arches are filled with big wheels that look to be 22s.

It's got a similar double-diamond pattern to the wide front grille, and the side intakes in the RS6's front bumper look even bigger than the RS5's. Camo is covering the headlights, which will get RS-specific running light designs and animations. There's a cute little lip spoiler on the trunk, and the rear diffuser has two gigantic oval exhaust tips. The taillights should also have RS designs.

The yellow sticker on the rear window confirms that the RS6 will be a plug-in hybrid, and while early rumors and prototypes pointed to the RS6 using the same twin-turbo V6 as the RS5, we know it will use an updated version of the Porsche-derived V8 that's in the current gas-only RS6 (and that's used in PHEV Porsches and Bentleys). With a large battery pack and an electric motor added on, the upcoming RS6 should have at least 700 horsepower and a usable EV range of a few dozen miles. We'll find out for sure when the RS6 debuts at some point in 2027.

Breaking: Joint Letter on the Revision of the CO₂ Emission Standards for Cars & Vans

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Counting combustion vehicles as clean would blur the market signal and bring back the very uncertainty that carmakers, suppliers, and investors cannot afford.
  • Dear Climate and Environment Ministers of the European Union,.
  • We, a broad coalition representing non-governmental organizations, think tanks, energy providers, renewable and cleantech industries, and the e-mobility sector, are writing to express our concern over the current direction of EU discussions on the revision of the cars and vans CO₂ emission standards regulation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Counting combustion vehicles as clean would blur the market signal and bring back the very uncertainty that carmakers, suppliers, and investors cannot afford. Manufacturers could meet their targets without selling a single electric car.

Dear Climate and Environment Ministers of the European Union,.

We, a broad coalition representing non-governmental organizations, think tanks, energy providers, renewable and cleantech industries, and the e-mobility sector, are writing to express our concern over the current direction of EU discussions on the revision of the cars and vans CO₂ emission standards regulation.

Road transport remains the primary driver of Europe’s oil dependency. This structural vulnerability costs the EU hundreds of billions of euros annually, weakens our economy, and leaves citizens exposed to geopolitical shocks. The second fossil fuel crisis in just four years has already added more than €50 billion to Europe’s energy bill, hitting households and businesses hard.

Our continued reliance on fossil fuels also accelerates the climate crisis. This summer, Europeans paid the price as successive heatwaves brought record temperatures, devastating wildfires, and severe droughts across the continent. Transport remains the EU’s biggest emitter, with cars and vans alone accounting for 16% of total CO₂ emissions.

Yet while the market is moving rapidly, political discussions are falling out of touch with reality.

Europe already has a mature, increasingly affordable and readily available structural solution in electric vehicles – which are also the most effective way to shield consumers from volatile fuel prices. Electric vehicles are scaling fast, reaching a record 27% market share in the third quarter of 2026 in the EU.

Industry observers note that instead of building on this momentum, discussions in the Council on the car CO₂ regulation threaten to slow the EV trajectory and inject uncertainty for companies and consumers. Most concerning is the proposal to create a newly introduced category for combustion cars running on e-fuels and biofuels, so-called “vehicles running exclusively on eligible fuels” (VEEFs), and count them as zero-emission vehicles.

Too much attention is being paid to combustion-based technologies, distracting from the electric future. Cars running on these fuels still burn fuel in a combustion engine; treating them on par with battery electric vehicles would create a false and unfair equivalence. Under this proposal, manufacturers could meet their targets without selling a single electric car.

It has been revealed that counting combustion vehicles as clean would blur the market signal and bring back the very uncertainty that carmakers, suppliers, and investors cannot afford. It would penalize businesses that are scaling up today and jeopardize the €200 billion already invested in the battery-electric transition. Europe cannot compete globally on electric cars if targets are weakened and undue credit is given to e-fuels, biofuels and hybrids.

In a recent development, we must reset this narrative on vehicle electrification. Europe’s clean industry needs investment certainty and regulatory stability. We therefore call on Climate and Environment Ministers to safeguard the car and van CO₂ targets adopted just three years ago, reject any weakening of the 2030 and 2035 ambition, and remove the “vehicles running exclusively on eligible fuels” (VEEFs) category.

It has been revealed that now is the time for political leadership. Member States have the chance to ensure this fossil fuel crisis is Europe’s last, and to act decisively to build a clean, sovereign, and affordable mobility system supported by a strong EU clean industry.

Download the letter to see the full list of signatories.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes
Florida court tosses Tampa General Hospital's suit against Eli Lilly over 340B discounts" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

A Florida federal court has tossed Tampa General Hospital's lawsuit against Eli Lilly over the 340B drug discount program.

In a recent development, florida's Middle District court dismissed the case on a motion from the drugmaker on Wednesday. If Tampa General Hospital wants to file an amended complaint, it must do so within 30 days.

The hospital initially sued the pharmaceutical company over a policy it implemented that requires providers to submit claims-level data on pharmacy and medical dispensing if they participate in 340B. Lilly said it would pull back discounts for providers that did not comply with the requirement and has done so for several organizations, drawing ire from the industry.

Tampa General said the decision is "unconscionable and immoral" in the initial complaint, filed in July.

Industry observers note that however, the district court argued that Supreme Court precedent holds that organizations like hospitals do not have the private right to sue if they have been charged beyond the threshold, based on a 2011 decision. SCOTUS stated that the right to sue was not outlined by Congress, so it is not an avenue available to these organizations.

"The Court made clear that there is simply no private remedy to superintend the pricing and provision of these discounted drugs," per the order.

"To permit this suit would be to encourage piecemeal litigation and defeat the [Supreme] Court’s insistence on maintaining the Congressional plan 'harmoniously and on a uniform, nationwide basis,'" according to the document.

Eli Lilly cheered the decision in a statement.

"Today’s decision is an notable step toward a more transparent 340B program," a Lilly spokesperson noted. "Lilly’s claims data requirement asks hospitals for basic information—information they already give insurers every day—to prevent unlawful duplicate discounts.".

"Decades of HRSA guidance and two federal appeals courts confirm that Lilly can lawfully require this information," the drugmaker noted. "More than 3,200 hospitals and clinics already share it with Lilly, and we hope Tampa General Hospital will join them.".

Tampa General Hospital has sued Eli Lilly and Organization over the drugmaker’s “unconscionable and immoral” rescindment of discounted pricing under the 340B program.

According to recent reports, the complaint, filed last week for the U.S. District Court in the Middle District of Florida, is early legal fallout from a policy Lilly implemented earlier this year that requires providers participating in the federal subsidy program to submit claims-level data for all pharmacy and medical dispensations. The company threatened to pull the discounts for those that didn’t comply and made good on its threat for a subset of hospitals last month, sparking outrage among provider groups.

According to recent reports, tampa General, a nearly 1,000-bed disproportionate share hospital, confirmed in the legal complaint that it was among those cut off. It is now spending 25% to 50% more on average for Lilly products, “many of which it must purchase because of Lilly’s status as the market’s only supplier of a given drug product.”.

Tampa General’s lawsuit frequently describes Lilly in such terms, framing the drugmaker as holding significant monopoly power and wielding it in violation of the Florida Deceptive and Unfair Trade Practices Act. It also often draws contrast to the 340B program’s intent to support the margins of safety-net hospitals providing care to vulnerable patients, against Lilly’s current status as the largest pharmaceutical company in the world by market cap.

A spokesperson for Lilly, in a statement given to Fierce Healthcare, described the lawsuit as “just another part of the broader hospital campaign to fight transparency and hide the fraud, waste and abuse that plague the 340B program.”.

Recent findings suggest that tampa General asked the court to order an immediate end to Lilly’s policy and to award damages for the higher prices to which the hospital was subjected. It contends Lilly’s alleged failure to comply with 340B pricing requirements and decision to continue marketing its products as 340B-discounted are unfair trade practices under the Florida statute.

“The most valuable pharmaceutical company in the world is engaged in a campaign to transfer dollars earmarked for charitable purposes into its own pocket,” the complaint reads. “The direct and inevitable result of Lilly’s actions is reduced healthcare for poor people. Its actions shock the conscience and are self-evidently unconscionable.”.

Tampa General, similar to the hospital associations that have protested Lilly’s policy, contends that the claims data it requires imposes substantial administrative burden on 340B providers. Even “hospitals who have caved to Lilly’s latest demands” have effectively had the prices for their covered outpatient drugs increased due to those administrative costs, it wrote in the complaint.

In a recent development, lilly and other drugmakers who have signaled similar aims have remarked they need claims data to spot instances in which a drug purchase is improperly granted multiple discounts under overlapping programs. The company has also disputed that the burden of its policy is as substantial as hospitals say.

“The claims data Lilly requires hospitals to share is information they already collect and send to insurers regularly,” the Lilly spokesperson noted of the lawsuit’s claims. “Refusing to share that same data with Lilly indicates that hospitals are more concerned with hiding rampant abuse in the program than improving its integrity. Lilly will keep working to ensure this program serves vulnerable patients instead of hospitals and their for-profit partners.”.

The 340B program has proven to be a magnet for industry and policy conflict, particularly in recent years as its scale has ballooned. The divide is most evident in the ongoing clash over a pilot rebate program that the Trump administration attempted to launch at the top of the year but was forced to restart after the hospital industry’s legal pushback.

340B providers also received a shock this past week when the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services floated a significant reduction in its 340B reimbursement to 33.4% below average sales price in its annual proposed rule on hospital outpatient payments.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 10:23 EST / NOVEMBER 24 2026.

Intelligent data infrastructure is becoming a priority as enterprises move artificial intelligence beyond isolated pilots and into production environments.

Industry observers note that the shift places newly introduced demands on storage systems built to support traditional applications, especially as organizations introduce AI workloads across hybrid and multicloud environments. NetApp Inc. is responding with a strategy that emphasizes infrastructure modernization without requiring enterprises to abandon existing investments, according to George Kurian (pictured), chief executive officer of NetApp.

In a recent development, “I think that the AI era requires organizations to be really good stewards of their data, because data is the foundation for knowledge and knowledge is the intellectual property,” he told theCUBE. “To have knowledge, you need really good intelligent data infrastructure that not only allows you to extract memory and context from your data, but also to keep it secure, well governed and a resource that you can trust.”.

Kurian spoke with theCUBE Research’s Christophe Bertrand and co-host Rebecca Knight during NetApp INSIGHT, in an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. The event’s coverage featured NetApp executives and technology partners discussing the evolving demands on enterprise data infrastructure and the challenges of bringing AI into production. (Disclosure below.).

Here’s theCUBE’s complete video discussion with George Kurian:.

Here are three insights you may have missed from theCUBE’s coverage of NetApp INSIGHT:.

It has been revealed that enterprise AI workloads are exposing limitations in storage architectures designed for more predictable application demands. NetApp’s Novus architecture separates data and metadata management so each can scale independently. The organization’s AI Data Engine is designed to discover, classify and prepare enterprise data for AI applications, according to Syam Nair, chief product officer of NetApp.

“Performance and throughput of accessing the data, that’s a necessity for AI, but that won’t be sufficient for agents to actually act on the data,” he remarked during the event. “If the data is not ready and it’s not protected, you get fast results. You get compromised results, but they may not be the ones you want.”.

The demands of AI factories are also changing how storage resources must be managed. NetApp’s approach aims to support high-throughput AI pipelines without sacrificing the responsiveness other applications require, according to Arindam Banerjee, chief platform and technology officer of NetApp, who spoke alongside Jason Hardy, vice president of storage technology at Nvidia Corp.

According to recent reports, “What happens is [that] different types of workloads like transactional workloads for metadata and heavy sequential workloads for, say, checkpoints, happen at the same time,” Banerjee told theCUBE. “Previous architectures did one or the other very well. They never were able to combine it and do both at the same time.”.

Here’s theCUBE’s complete video interview with Jason Hardy and Arindam Banerjee:.

Modernizing enterprise infrastructure often requires organizations to accommodate existing applications while introducing new AI capabilities. NetApp and Oracle Corp. are addressing that challenge through a co-engineered, fully managed storage service that runs ONTAP natively within Oracle Cloud Infrastructure. The offering is designed to ease migration of existing ONTAP workloads without requiring application redesign, according to Konstantinos Papamiltiadis, senior vice president of partnerships at Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, a division of Oracle.

Recent findings suggest that “When I’m going into the OCI console, I have the option to use the ONTAP as a native service,” he told theCUBE. “For me, the most important thing that we managed to build is, from an operational perspective, we bring everything under one single interface that provides simplicity and consistency.”.

According to recent reports, netApp and Oracle Corp. are extending enterprise storage capabilities into the public cloud through a co-engineered, fully managed service that runs ONTAP natively within Oracle Cloud Infrastructure. The offering is designed to ease migration of existing ONTAP workloads without requiring application redesign, according to Konstantinos Papamiltiadis, senior vice president of partnerships at Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, a division of Oracle.

It has been revealed that “When I’m going into the OCI console, I have the option to use the ONTAP as a native service,” he told theCUBE. “For me, the most important thing that we managed to build is, from an operational perspective, we bring everything under one single interface that provides simplicity and consistency.”.

In a recent development, the integration challenge extends beyond cloud storage to the networking and compute resources that support AI workloads. NetApp and Cisco Systems Inc. are expanding their FlexPod infrastructure with validated designs intended to reduce deployment complexity. The partnership has served 10,000 customers over 16 years, according to James Cole, vice president of data center networking, business development, partnerships and go-to-market at Cisco, and Alvaro Celis, chief partner and ecosystem officer at NetApp.

Industry observers note that “Twenty years ago, 10 years ago, you would’ve been designing your data structures and your applications around the infrastructure. Now we’ve turned that on its head,” Cole stated during the event. “You’re really designing the infrastructure around the movement of data. Who better to do that together than the person you trust with your data and the person you trust with your network?”.

Another partnership focuses on private AI deployment and measurable business outcomes. The NetApp AIPod Mini combines NetApp infrastructure with the Generate platform from Iterate Studio Inc., doing business as Iterate.ai, according to Brian Sathianathan, co-founder and chief technology officer of Iterate.ai. In one insurance deployment cited during the discussion, an agent reduced accident-report analysis from approximately eight hours to eight minutes.

“AIPod Mini has attached connections to the NetApp storage, and it talks to NetApp using the ONTAP protocol that’s time-tested,” he said during the event. “Then, on top of the AIPod Mini, we are running our Generate software. That software has a [large language model] embedded in it, so you can run all your AI queries locally and fully privately within your four walls.”.

A 19-year study reveals a troubling link between napping and death

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1150 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A daily nap may seem like a harmless way to recharge, but upcoming research suggests that certain napping habits could provide crucial clues about a person's health as they age.
  • Researchers from Mass General Brigham and Rush University Medical Center examined the napping patterns of 1,338 older adults over a period of up to 19 years.
  • "Excessive napping later in life has been linked to neurodegeneration, cardiovascular diseases and even greater morbidity, but many of those findings rely on self-reported napping habits and leave out metrics like when and how regular those naps are," noted lead author Chenlu Gao, PhD, an investigator in the Department of Anesthesiology at Mass General Brigham and an affiliated research fellow in the Division of Sleep and Circadian Disorders in the Department of Medicine.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A daily nap may seem like a harmless way to recharge, but upcoming research suggests that certain napping habits could provide crucial clues about a person's health as they age. Scientists have found that taking longer or more frequent naps, particularly in the morning, is associated with an increased risk of death among older adults.

Researchers from Mass General Brigham and Rush University Medical Center examined the napping patterns of 1,338 older adults over a period of up to 19 years. Their findings, published in JAMA Network Open, suggest that monitoring daytime sleep could help identify underlying medical conditions or early signs of declining health.

"Excessive napping later in life has been linked to neurodegeneration, cardiovascular diseases and even greater morbidity, but many of those findings rely on self-reported napping habits and leave out metrics like when and how regular those naps are," noted lead author Chenlu Gao, PhD, an investigator in the Department of Anesthesiology at Mass General Brigham and an affiliated research fellow in the Division of Sleep and Circadian Disorders in the Department of Medicine. "Our study is one of the first to show an association between objectively measured nap patterns and mortality and suggests there is immense clinical value in tracking napping patterns to catch health conditions early.".

Why Scientists Are Studying Daytime Napping.

Daytime naps are common among older adults, with estimates suggesting that 20% to 60% regularly nap. An occasional nap can help restore energy and improve alertness, but excessive daytime sleeping in later life has been associated with several health concerns.

Despite these connections, researchers still have an incomplete understanding of how specific napping behaviors relate to long-term health. Many earlier studies depended on participants remembering and reporting their own sleep habits, which may not provide an accurate picture. They also often overlooked important details, such as how long naps lasted, when they occurred, and how much napping patterns changed from one day to the next.

According to recent reports, to obtain more reliable measurements, the research team analyzed information from the Rush Memory and Aging Project. Debuted in 1997, this long-running study was designed primarily to investigate memory, thinking abilities, and neurological decline among older adults in northern Illinois, most of whom were white.

Starting in 2005, participants wore wrist activity monitors for 10 days to record their daily periods of rest and movement. Researchers used these measurements to identify daytime sleep and assess nap duration, frequency, timing, and daily variation.

Longer and More Frequent Naps Linked to Higher Mortality Risk.

By 2025, researchers had assembled up to 19 years of follow-up information from 1,338 participants. They then examined whether napping habits measured during the initial assessment were associated with the likelihood of dying from any cause during the subsequent years.

The results revealed several notable patterns. Older adults who slept longer during the day or took naps more frequently had higher mortality rates. The timing of naps also appeared to matter.

Each additional hour spent napping per day was associated with approximately a 13% higher mortality risk. Taking one additional nap per day was linked to about a 7% increase in risk.

It has been revealed that one of the most striking findings involved morning naps. Participants who napped in the morning had a 30% higher mortality risk compared with those who napped in the afternoon.

Industry observers note that however, not every aspect of napping was associated with poorer outcomes. Researchers found no increased mortality risk linked to irregular napping schedules, suggesting that changes in nap timing or duration from day to day were not necessarily indicators of greater risk.

Could Napping Habits Reveal Hidden Health Problems?

According to recent reports, the researchers emphasize that their findings do not mean daytime naps directly cause health problems or shorten lives. Instead, excessive napping may reflect medical conditions or changes in the body that have not yet been recognized.

"It is notable to note that this is correlation, not causation. Excessive napping is likely indicating underlying disease, chronic conditions, sleep disturbances, or circadian dysregulation," mentioned Gao. "Now that we know there is a strong correlation between napping patterns and mortality rates, we can make the case to implement wearable daytime nap assessments to predict health conditions and prevent further decline.".

These findings raise the possibility that wearable activity trackers could eventually become useful tools for monitoring health in older adults. By identifying changes in daytime sleep habits, healthcare professionals might be able to recognize warning signs of underlying illness, disrupted sleep cycles, or neurological decline earlier.

Although further research is needed to determine how effectively napping patterns can predict specific medical conditions, the study suggests that something as ordinary as a daily nap could provide valuable information about a person's overall health.

Study Authorship, Disclosures, and Funding.

Recent findings suggest that authorship: In addition to Gao and Li, the Mass General Brigham researchers involved in the study include Ruixue Cai, Xi Zheng, Arlen Gaba, Lei Gao, and Kun Hu. Other contributors include Lei Yu, Aron S. Buchman, and David A. Bennett.

In a recent development, disclosures: Li received a financial gift from iFutureLab to support research and has received consulting payments for serving on the iFutureLab-HEKA Scientific Advisory Board as Chair of Cardiac Dynamics and Honorary Life-Time Co-Founder. Li also received an honorarium for delivering a lecture at Shandong University.

Industry observers note that hu has received consulting fees for serving on the iFutureLab-HEKA Scientific Advisory Board as Chair of Medical Biodynamics and Honorary Life-Time Co-Founder. Mass General Brigham reviewed and managed the interests of both Li and Hu under its conflict of interest policies. These interests are unrelated to the present research.

Funding: The research received support from the American Academy of Sleep Medicine Foundation (290-FP-22), the Alzheimer's Association Research Fellowship to Promote Diversity (AARFD-22-928372), and the National Institute on Aging (RF1AG064312; R01AG083799).

Recent findings suggest that gao C. received additional funding from the National Heart Lung and Blood Institute (5T32HL007901). Li received support from the BrightFocus Foundation (A2020886S) and startup funding from the Department of Anesthesia, Critical Care and Pain Medicine at Massachusetts General Hospital. Hu also received startup funding from the same department.

Sources indicate that gao L. received additional support from the Alzheimer's Association (AACSF-23-1148490), National Institute on Aging (R03AG087439), American Academy of Sleep Medicine (352-DS-24), and National Institute of General Medical Sciences (R35GM160254).

The Rush Memory and Aging Project was funded by the National Institutes of Health (R01AG056352 and R01AG017917).
