Cigna Group Foundation making $31.5M in grants available to community organizations in 10 states" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Cigna is making $31.5 million in grant funding available over the next three years to nonprofits in 10 states that are aiming to tackle several key community health priorities.

The company said that funds will be made available through its philanthropic arm, the Cigna Group Foundation, with applications open now through Dec. 18. Cigna said in an announcement that it's looking for organizations tackling youth mental health, veteran wellness and the impact of complex health needs on patients and their caregivers.

Cigna stated the program seeks to deepen the firm's community health strategy to address critical challenges.

It has been revealed that the tech giant first released a newly introduced approach to community health and engagement in 2024, and since then has deployed more than $30 million in funding to 190 nonprofit organizations. Projects backed by these grants have reached at least 321,000 people, Cigna stated.

"Over the past several years, we’ve seen the tangible impact we can make when we invest in strong nonprofit partners and come together to help communities achieve better health and vitality," mentioned Melissa Skottegaard, board chair of The Cigna Group Foundation, in the announcement. "We’re building on what’s working, bringing together funding, collaboration and the skills of our employee volunteers to address some of the most pressing health challenges facing communities across the street and around the world.".

Cigna will allot $10.5 million to each of the three focus areas under the initiative, per the announcement. Youth mental health, for example, has been a leading topic at the organization for some time, and the company mentioned it will also continue to build on its partnership with the Boys and Girls Clubs of America in this area.

Industry observers note that in that partnership, Cigna has helped build out trauma-informed care services to 90% of clubs, reaching 11,000 employees. The company stated that these efforts have supported 1,600 youths, and that its workforce has contributed more than 2,000 hours to local clubs.

According to recent reports, eligible organizations can apply for two-year, $250,000 grants to support programs in the three categories. The funds will be available to groups in Arizona, Connecticut, Florida, Georgia, Illinois, Missouri, New Jersey, Pennsylvania, Tennessee and Texas, per the announcement.

Cigna mentioned its foundation will also continue to support community health through its Health Equity Impact Fund.

"Community organizations can be a powerful source of support for people navigating complex health conditions,” mentioned Matt Perlberg, president of Evernorth Pharmacy & Care Delivery and board member of the Cigna Group Foundation, in the announcement. “By helping patients and caregivers connect with resources and overcome barriers to care, these organizations can provide notable support alongside essential medical treatment, helping people navigate their health and care journey.”.

Scientists find a simple daily routine linked to less pain and depression

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1015 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A consistent daily routine may do more for your health than you realize.
  • In a recent development, the findings suggest that everyday habits, such as waking up, eating meals, socializing, and going to bed at consistent times, may play an notable role in physical and mental well-being.
  • Sources indicate that the discovery could be especially crucial for older adults, who frequently experience sleep difficulties.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A consistent daily routine may do more for your health than you realize. Researchers at the University of Missouri have found that older adults who follow regular daily schedules tend to experience less physical pain and fewer symptoms of depression, even when they struggle to get a good night's sleep.

In a recent development, the findings suggest that everyday habits, such as waking up, eating meals, socializing, and going to bed at consistent times, may play an notable role in physical and mental well-being. By helping the body maintain its natural internal clock, a predictable routine could offer health benefits that extend beyond improved sleep.

Sources indicate that the discovery could be especially crucial for older adults, who frequently experience sleep difficulties. According to the National Council on Aging, roughly half of adults age 60 and older report symptoms of insomnia, a condition that can make it difficult to fall asleep, stay asleep, or get restful sleep.

Daily Routines Linked to Less Pain and Depression.

It has been revealed that to investigate the relationship between sleep, daily habits, and overall health, Eunjin Tracy, an assistant professor in the College of Education and Human Development at the University of Missouri, examined survey responses from 67 older adults. Among the participants, 37 reported experiencing insomnia.

Industry observers note that as researchers expected, those with insomnia generally reported more physical pain and higher levels of depression than participants without the condition. However, another pattern emerged when Tracy examined their daily routines.

Participants who maintained more consistent schedules tended to report less pain and fewer depressive symptoms, regardless of their sleep quality. This suggests that keeping regular daily habits may be associated with better health even when sleep problems persist.

"Regardless of sleep quality, those who reported having a regular daily routine had lower levels of physical pain and less depression compared to those without a daily routine," Tracy mentioned. "If we are consistent with when we wake up, eat, work or study, interact with others and go to bed, those time cues help synchronize our internal body clocks. Over the long term, that seems to be linked with improved health outcomes.".

Why Your Body's Internal Clock Matters.

Recent findings suggest that one possible explanation involves the circadian rhythm, the body's natural 24-hour timing system. This internal clock helps coordinate when we feel awake or sleepy and influences numerous biological processes, including hormone activity, metabolism, and mood.

Sources indicate that rather than operating independently of our surroundings, the circadian system responds to signals that help it keep time. Light and darkness are especially notable, but regular activities such as eating, working, interacting with others, and sleeping can also provide timing cues.

Industry observers note that when these signals follow a predictable pattern, they help keep the body's biological rhythms aligned. Irregular schedules, on the other hand, can interfere with that coordination.

"When we regulate our circadian rhythm well, our bodies function well, but if it gets too distracted, our bodies don't function as well," Tracy said.

Although the study did not establish that regular routines directly reduce pain or depression, the findings point to circadian regulation as one possible explanation for the connection.

The Hidden Effects of Social Jet Lag.

According to recent reports, even relatively small changes in daily schedules may disrupt the body's internal clock. One common example is social jet lag, which occurs when a person's sleep schedule shifts between workdays and days off.

It has been revealed that someone who wakes up early throughout the week but stays up late and sleeps in on weekends may experience this mismatch. The resulting disruption resembles some of the effects of traveling across time zones, even though the person has never left home.

Tracy suggests that maintaining reasonably consistent schedules throughout the entire week, including weekends, may help limit these disruptions and support healthier circadian rhythms.

"As someone who wakes up and goes to bed at the same time every day, I think a daily routine can be helpful for people of all ages across their lifespan," Tracy said. "There is growing awareness about the concept of social jet lag -- waking up and going to bed at different times on weekends compared to weekdays -- and the disruptions it causes to our circadian rhythm, so hopefully this research helps more people consider the health benefits of a daily routine. Since one-third of our lives will be spent sleeping, I think health and well-being research should be looked at holistically from a 24-hour perspective and not just focus on when we are awake.".

A Simple Habit With Potential Health Benefits.

The research highlights an aspect of healthy living that can be easy to overlook. While getting enough quality sleep remains important, the consistency of activities throughout the day may also be connected to how people feel physically and emotionally.

Because the study relied on survey data from a relatively small group of older adults, it cannot prove that adopting a regular routine will relieve pain or depression. Larger studies would be needed to establish whether changing daily schedules directly improves these outcomes.

Still, the findings suggest that a predictable daily routine may be a useful component of a broader approach to health, particularly for people experiencing insomnia.

For older adults and potentially people of other ages, simple habits such as maintaining regular waking times, eating meals on a consistent schedule, and limiting major changes in weekend sleep patterns may help support the body's natural rhythms.

The study, "Behavioral-social rhythms and insomnia symptoms: associations with pain, body mass index, and depressive symptoms among older adults," was published in the Journal of Behavioral Medicine.

HLTH 2026: Elsevier upgrades ClinicalKey AI with full patient EHR context" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Elsevier unveiled this week a major upgrade to ClinicalKey AI, enabling the AI-powered clinical decision support tool to access a patient’s full electronic health record and evaluate treatment prepares against the tech giant’s evidence-based medical library.

As AI advances, Elsevier has strategically shifted from a traditional academic publisher—it’s one of the world's largest publishers of scientific, technical and medical content—to an AI-driven analytics information company, incorporating generative and agentic AI into its healthcare and academic research.

Recent findings suggest that clinicalKey AI is a HIPAA-ready point-of-care decision support tool that draws answers from articles sourced from approximately 1,000 world-leading journals. Elsevier’s upgraded ClinicalKey AI is already deployed at more than 1,200 hospitals, and the company claims the solution integrates with all EHR providers. Elsevier recently struck a content agreement with the JAMA Network that brings full-text content and visuals from the JAMA Network Family of Journals to ClinicalKey AI.

ClinicalKey AI was originally co-developed through a strategic partnership between Elsevier and OpenEvidence. An Elsevier spokesperson said the company's collaboration with OpenEvidence on ClinicalKey AI has concluded.

Industry observers note that the organization has rapidly expanded its AI capabilities and features, including ClinicalKey Nursing AI, an AI-powered tool built specifically for nurses and nursing workflows. Elsevier has also developed specialized AI assistants, such as LeapSpace, an AI-assisted workspace for researchers that’s built on 15+ million peer-reviewed articles and book content and 100 million Scopus records, according to the company.

It has been revealed that three months ago, the manufacturer rolled out its "Ask AI" feature across more than 1,500 U.S. hospital sites using its flagship ClinicalKey platform. With the generative AI feature, clinicians can ask conversational clinical questions and receive direct, cited answers drawn from evidence-based sources, including premium journals and content from leading medical organizations, the company remarked. Unlike general-purpose chatbots, Ask AI does not pull from the open web and does not store, process or retain patient-identifiable information, according to the company.

In a move to develop context-aware AI, the company acquired Wellsheet in June. The health technology company aggregates and synthesizes patient chart data—including notes, labs, imaging and medication orders—from EHRs to provide relevant clinical intelligence at the bedside.

“The problem we’re trying to solve here is that physicians are challenged by so many things when they’re taking care of patients; top among them is patient complexity. Patients have more and more conditions, and they’re taking more and more medications. It can be hard to really understand the full picture and determine how to proceed,” Dr. Claudine Lott, physician executive for clinical solutions at Elsevier, told Fierce Healthcare during the HLTH conference this week.

“Our original ClinicalKey AI tool has been a place where the clinician can go, and they can ask a question, and it searches this curated database of evidence-based content we’ve given it and gives them an answer. But there was a bit of a missing piece in that it wasn’t capturing that patient context. If you wanted to get an answer, that’s really tailored to a patient, it was limited to what you can type in,” she stated.

She added, “Wellsheet has 10 years of experience with looking at the entirety of the patient chart and helping to surface that to the clinician.”.

There is a growing market for AI-powered clinical decision support products, but Elsevier contends its advantage lies in its depth of patient context and its large, curated content base, with a wholly owned, large proprietary library of peer-reviewed STM literature, including content from millions of articles, journals and books.

Industry observers note that san Juan Regional Medical Center in Farmington, Newly introduced Mexico, is using ClinicalKey AI’s new patient context functionality to provide quality care with fewer resources. With smaller clinical and quality teams than large academic health systems, and in a state where nearly 40% of residents rely on Medicaid, the medical center, which serves the Four Corners area, has found this support especially valuable, according to Carlo Hallak, M.D., physician executive, information services, at San Juan Regional Medical Center.

A non-profit, community-owned acute care hospital and Level III trauma center, San Juan Regional Medical Center operates outpatient and specialty clinics alongside its main hospital campus, San Juan Regional Rehabilitation Hospital and San Juan Health Partners clinics.

Hallak emphasized that Elsevier is a primary source of medical knowledge rather than a “wrapper” for other AI platforms, and that was a key distinction for the organization, he said. And ClinicalKey AI is designed for the entire care team. “The hospital is run by nurses, mid-level providers, other caregiver teams,” he told Fierce Healthcare at the HLTH conference.

The medical center aims to move clinicians to enterprise LLMs integrated with the electronic health record that can provide the full patient context, Hallak noted.

Recent findings suggest that "We're already seeing how ClinicalKey AI can be instrumental at the bedside and help improve care for our patients. As a rural healthcare center, we are proud to say that by using ClinicalKey AI to check each patient’s care against the same evidence base that major health systems rely on, we’re able to deliver the standard of care patients expect in any major city or leading academic center," Hallak said.

He added, "ClinicalKey AI reads the whole chart, checks it against the evidence and indicates exactly where each finding comes from. That support is invaluable for a hospital like ours, and we’re already seeing strong adoption of ClinicalKey AI among our clinicians.".

Hallak cited an example of a physician who used ClinicalKey AI to correctly identify viral meningitis, preventing an aggressive and unnecessary treatment course for bacterial meningitis.

Sources indicate that clinicalKey AI supports the physician’s judgment rather than replacing it, helping the clinician get to relevant evidence faster, he mentioned, noting that, in the case of the viral meningitis patient, the physician’s clinical judgment was critical in recognizing that something was unusual and then consulting colleagues. The AI tool then helped accelerate the next step by quickly surfacing information the clinician otherwise would have found by searching the medical literature.

Physicians also use the tool during weekly complex case discussions to promptly review trending medications, images and test results in one summarized sheet, he noted.

“It’s going to expedite a lot of the work they do when it comes to these complex cases,” he said.

The AI solution can swiftly summarize a complex patient history at the point of care, and this can help care teams in the emergency department understand a frequent ED patient, Hallak remarked.

One patient has visited their emergency department 95 times in less than a year, in addition to making numerous visits to neighboring health systems, Hallak noted. When that patient arrives, clinicians who aren't familiar with him would traditionally have to dig through the chart to understand his history. With Elsevier's ClinicalKey AI tool, they can ask for a summary of the patient's recent visits and care and get that information within seconds, he noted.

Because patients who frequently visit hospital EDs typically receive care at multiple organizations, San Juan Regional Medical Center is also working with other local health systems on interoperability efforts so clinicians can get a more complete picture of what happened during the patient's visits across different facilities.

As a rural hospital with staffing constraints, technology is essential to filling workforce gaps and supporting care delivery, Hallak contends.

Recent findings suggest that "We don't have enough physicians, enough nurses, enough transporters, enough caregivers. We will never be able to have enough of those," he remarked.

Hallak envisions ClinicalKey AI will be particularly valuable for discharging patients from the hospital faster.

Sources indicate that generative AI tools can help speed up patient discharges by identifying barriers, assessing patients’ care needs and providing relevant information from both structured and unstructured data. Because the platform is designed for the broader care team, case managers and physicians can access the same information, while push notifications can alert clinicians when test results are available so they can act swiftly, Hallak said.

"From an operational perspective, it allows for this care team coordination of care, and also from a physician perspective, it provides the context whenever there's something hanging and they're trying to understand more what's happening with the patient['s] discharge. You could be a hospitalist, and you've been off shift for like seven days, and then you come to the hospital and now the patient is on their tenth day, but you inherit that discharge. Going through, reading every progress note for every single day, reading every consult for every subspecialty that looked at this patient usually would take two to three days to actually get the patient out of the building safely," he said.

Rather than manually compiling information for a discharge summary, clinicians can use ClinicalKey AI to aggregate relevant information from across the patient’s record, trace it back to its source and review the AI-generated summary before signing off on the discharge, according to Hallak.

"It is a game changer, in my opinion. One of our hospitals said it used to take me three days to discharge a patient; now it takes me less than three hours," he said.

Going forward, the system expects to measure operational outcomes such as length of stay, safe discharge and multidisciplinary-rounds use, according to Hallak. The medical center also plans to evaluate clinicians' use of the tool and how it changes care decisions.

The medical center has also deployed other AI tools such as Oracle Health's clinical AI agent for ambient documentation.

Industry observers note that "These things are crucial. We're hoping to bring in a clinical AI agent for nurses as well to help the whole care team be able to eliminate the noise, the friction that typically EHRs or IT would bring to the conversation," Hallak noted.

The medical center is taking a risk-based approach to AI governance, using source verification and peer review for AI-generated summaries while applying greater scrutiny to tools that are predictive or suggestive, Hallak noted. That oversight involves clinical experts as well as compliance, legal and cybersecurity teams along with traditional vendor security and product-vetting requirements.

AI governance should become stricter as the technology moves from summarizing information to recommending or taking actions, he remarked.

Elsevier designed ClinicalKey AI with security and trust in mind, including HIPAA compliance, citations that show where information comes from and safeguards that keep the tool from prescribing what clinicians should do. Instead, it surfaces relevant information to help clinicians make their own decisions, Lott mentioned.

"Health systems tell us two things stand in the way of adopting AI: tools that don’t work with their existing EHR partners, and concerns about security, compliance and responsible use," Omry Bigger, president of Clinical Solutions at Elsevier, said. "ClinicalKey AI was designed to address both. As an EHR-supported and HIPAA-compliant ready solution, ClinicalKey AI integrates seamlessly across health systems to provide clinicians with trusted evidence and patient context that gives them tailored clinical insights for each patient at the point of care.".

Consumers believe AI will be key in making healthcare simpler: survey" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Americans want a healthcare experience that's simpler and easier to understand, and artificial intelligence may be the key to getting there, a new survey reveals.

The poll, conducted by the Harris Poll and commissioned by Elevance Health, found that 82% of American patients view at least some part of healthcare information as a "foreign language," and close to half (45%) remarked they made a healthcare decision they later regretted due to a lack of understanding.

The survey was conducted among 2,0001 adults in mid-July, and 74% noted they have encountered a key barrier, such as understanding their health insurance or a medical bill. And only a quarter (27%) said they completely understand their own health coverage.

That mentioned, most (79%) of those surveyed said they believe AI can help to improve the healthcare experience overall.

Ratnakar Lavu, chief digital information officer at Elevance Health, told Fierce in an email that because the tech has the ability to quickly surface and parse key data about a member or health need, it can serve as a central piece of the puzzle in making a more personalized experience.

Recent findings suggest that "AI-enabled tools give us the ability to create a unique member context," he noted. "Because of this digital technology, we can now truly 'know the person' and proactively work with them to help them manage their healthcare needs.".

For example, 82% of those surveyed mentioned they would like to receive answers about healthcare as swiftly as they can use an app to order a food delivery, and 83% would like to easily access recommendations that pull from their health coverage, individual health needs and financial situation.

Seventy-two percent said they would trust AI for accuracy on at least one type of information, such as an explanation of benefits, cost estimates or details on medication.

It has been revealed that however, while many Americans believe AI can play a leading role in driving a better health experience, just 20% noted they currently use the tech regularly as a source of information. And while 72% said they trusted the tech to surface key health information, 33% said they would trust an AI platform to translate their insurance benefits, and 30% said they trust the tech to estimate care costs.

Just 13% stated they would trust AI to make diagnoses.

Lavu said that healthcare organizations looking to roll out upcoming tools need to avoid simply embedding AI into programs for the sake of it, and be transparent about both the use case as well as the role of the human in the loop.

The study also found that women were less likely than men to trust AI, and younger generations were more likely to use it as a source of healthcare information than older groups.

In a recent development, "We have to implement AI at the speed of trust, which means being thoughtful about where AI adds value, not just delivering technology for technology’s sake," he mentioned. "Trust is also earned when AI-enabled programs truly make things easier for the consumer. ".

For example, Elevance Health has deployed an AI-powered program to support utilization management reviews and help drive faster approvals where possible, though AI is not used to make claims denials. It is also leaning on AI for more proactive member engagement initiatives through its digital channels, identifying individuals that would benefit from extra support or who may face gaps in care.

"We start by listening to members and identifying where healthcare is creating the most confusion or friction," Lavu said. "From there, we determine the right solution, which may or may not involve AI. When AI is the right tool, it should fit naturally into familiar interactions and make it easier for members to get an answer or take the next step.".

A simple supplement could help your immune system fight cancer and viral infections

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1825 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, A common amino acid found in everyday foods could play a surprisingly notable role in helping the immune system recognize cancer and fight viral infections.
  • Arginine is an amino acid that the body produces naturally and also obtains from protein-rich foods.
  • Industry observers note that now, new research suggests that restoring arginine levels could help the immune system respond more effectively to serious threats.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, A common amino acid found in everyday foods could play a surprisingly notable role in helping the immune system recognize cancer and fight viral infections. Scientists at Rockefeller University have discovered that when the body runs low on arginine, a key part of its immune defense system can stop working properly, potentially allowing dangerous cells and viruses to escape detection.

Arginine is an amino acid that the body produces naturally and also obtains from protein-rich foods. It is essential for making proteins that perform countless functions throughout the body. Researchers have long known that unusually low arginine levels are associated with several diseases, including colon cancer, but exactly how this shortage affects the body's defenses has remained unclear.

Industry observers note that now, new research suggests that restoring arginine levels could help the immune system respond more effectively to serious threats. In experiments involving mice, increasing dietary arginine reduced the formation of colon cancer tumors and lessened the severity of influenza and SARS-CoV-2 infections. Remarkably, providing arginine after mice had already contracted influenza also improved their outcomes.

The findings, published in the journal Cell, raise the possibility that an inexpensive, readily available supplement could eventually become a useful addition to cancer treatments and strategies for combating viral infections. However, further research in humans is needed to determine whether the benefits observed in mice translate into effective treatments for people.

How a Missing Nutrient Could Help Cancer Escape the Immune System.

Recent findings suggest that the research was led by Sohail Tavazoie, who directs the Elizabeth and Vincent Meyer Laboratory of Systems Cancer Biology at Rockefeller University. His team has spent years investigating how arginine influences cancer development and progression.

Industry observers note that in 2023, the researchers discovered that depriving colon cancer cells of arginine caused them to accumulate more genetic mutations. These changes can contribute to the unpredictable behavior of cancer cells, raising important questions about how arginine shortages might influence the disease.

Industry observers note that the latest study reveals another potentially significant consequence. When arginine becomes scarce, cells struggle to produce enough of a crucial immune system protein known as MHC-1. This protein acts as a warning system, helping immune cells identify potential dangers such as cancerous changes or viral infections.

Without enough MHC-1, abnormal or infected cells may become harder for the immune system to recognize.

Encouragingly, the researchers also found that supplying a moderate amount of arginine, comparable to the quantity available in a couple of over-the-counter supplement tablets, could help restore production of this important protein.

It has been revealed that "Our work reveals how a lack of arginine interferes with the immune system, and suggests that upping arginine intake could prove beneficial," states first author Qiushuang Wu, a postdoc in the lab. "Perhaps that means it could be used in combination with other therapies to treat both cancer and viral infections.".

"Arginine supplementation could be readily tested in patients receiving immunotherapies or given to high-risk populations exposed to viral pathogens," Tavazoie suggests. "Considering that arginine is inexpensive and readily available, we hope that therapeutic and preventative studies could be undertaken soon.".

The Surprising Connection Between Arginine and Immune Defenses.

To understand why arginine has such an vital effect, the researchers investigated how cells use amino acids to manufacture proteins.

Proteins are built from amino acids according to genetic instructions encoded in DNA. These instructions are copied into messenger RNA, which carries the information to the cellular machinery responsible for protein production.

The instructions are read in groups of three genetic letters called codons. Each codon specifies an amino acid or provides another signal needed during protein production. Arginine is unusual in that six different codons can specify it, reflecting the multiple ways its incorporation into proteins can be encoded.

In a recent development, scientists already knew that changes in amino acid availability could affect cellular metabolism and signaling, two processes that help regulate how cells obtain energy and respond to their surroundings. What remained less clear was whether shortages of particular amino acids could directly influence which proteins cells produce.

To investigate, Wu examined the effects of arginine availability across several disease models, including colon cancer, influenza, and SARS-CoV-2. Each of these diseases has previously been associated with abnormal levels of various amino acids.

The research was supported in part by the Stavros Niarchos Foundation (SNF) Institute for Global Infectious Disease Research at The Rockefeller University and the Weill Cancer East Hub.

"One of the most dramatic patterns to emerge was that arginine was the most depleted amino acid in all of these diseases," she claims.

Why Low Arginine Levels Can Disrupt the Immune System.

In laboratory experiments using cultured cells, Wu examined how arginine shortages affected protein production. She identified 414 proteins whose levels dropped abnormally when arginine was scarce.

It has been revealed that many of these proteins were associated with biological functions already known to depend on arginine. However, the researchers uncovered a more unexpected effect involving three genes from the HLA family.

These genes provide instructions for producing proteins associated with MHC-I (major histocompatibility complex class I), an essential component of the immune system's ability to recognize threats.

MHC-I proteins are displayed on the surfaces of cells throughout the body. They act somewhat like identification displays, presenting small fragments of proteins from inside the cell to immune cells known as T cells.

When these displays reveal suspicious material, such as proteins produced by a virus or abnormal proteins associated with cancer, T cells can recognize the danger and help coordinate an immune response.

But the researchers found that arginine deficiency interfered with the production of these molecular warning signals.

Industry observers note that the reason involved ribosomes, the tiny cellular machines that assemble proteins by following genetic instructions. Because the proteins involved in MHC-I production require arginine at numerous points, the researchers suspected that an insufficient supply could interfere with their assembly.

Further experiments confirmed that suspicion. When arginine was unavailable, ribosomes stalled while trying to manufacture MHC-I proteins. Without enough of the required amino acid, the cells could not efficiently complete the process.

Sources indicate that as a result, fewer MHC-I proteins reached the cell surface, reducing the signals that would normally alert T cells to cancer-associated or viral proteins. This created an opportunity for dangerous cells to avoid immune detection.

"These findings are exciting because they reveal that consumption of a specific amino acid can directly regulate gene expression in an organism by increasing production of a protein enriched in that amino acid," Tavazoie says. "We believe that such selective translational tuning of gene expression through dietary manipulation likely extends to many other proteins and amino acids.".

More Arginine Meant Fewer Colon Cancer Tumors in Mice.

After identifying the molecular mechanism, Wu investigated whether changing the amount of arginine in an animal's diet could influence disease outcomes.

It has been revealed that mice receiving diets low in arginine developed more colon cancer tumors. In contrast, mice consuming higher amounts of the amino acid developed fewer tumors.

These findings provided evidence that arginine availability can influence cancer development through its effects on the immune system, rather than simply changing how individual cancer cells behave.

The results also raised a broader question: If arginine helps immune cells recognize cancer, could it provide similar benefits when the body encounters dangerous viruses?

Arginine Also Improved Outcomes From Influenza and COVID-19 Viruses.

To explore that possibility, Wu collaborated with Heinz-Heinrich Hoffman, a research assistant professor in Charles Rice's Laboratory of Virology and Infectious Disease.

Together, they examined the effects of dietary arginine in mouse models of influenza and SARS-CoV-2, the virus responsible for COVID-19.

Industry observers note that the findings followed the same general pattern seen in the colon cancer experiments. Mice consuming more arginine experienced less severe symptoms from viral infections, suggesting that adequate levels of the amino acid helped support the body's immune defenses.

The researchers then made an even more surprising discovery.

According to recent reports, arginine did not appear to be beneficial only when consumed before an infection. Giving mice additional arginine after they had already been infected with influenza also improved their outcomes.

"Not only did mice with an arginine-rich diet have milder symptoms from viral infections, giving the mice arginine after influenza infection improved their outcomes too," Wu notes. "That was very surprising. From our genetic models, we knew manipulating arginine levels had a strong effect on gene expression, but we didn't expect the dietary manipulation to be equally impactful.".

The observation suggests that changing nutrient availability might influence how the immune system responds even after a viral infection has taken hold.

Could a Simple Supplement Improve Cancer and Virus Treatments?

The discovery has potentially important implications for understanding why some people become more vulnerable to cancer and severe viral infections.

It has been revealed that arginine levels naturally decline with age, and inadequate nutrition can further reduce the amount available to cells. The researchers suspect that these changes may contribute to the weakening of immune defenses seen in certain diseases and in older adults.

It has been revealed that "Qiushuang's findings illuminate how poor diet and aging -- during which arginine levels naturally decline -- could create the perfect storm for the initiation of colon cancer. Similarly, age-related arginine loss could partially contribute to the greater mortality caused by respiratory viruses," Tavazoie notes. "We're also investigating whether making dietary changes in other amino acids has beneficial effects in a variety of disease contexts. There are no doubt more discoveries to come.".

The possibility of using arginine alongside existing cancer immunotherapies is particularly intriguing. These treatments work by helping the immune system recognize and attack cancer cells. If low arginine levels interfere with the molecular signals required for that recognition, restoring the nutrient might help some treatments work more effectively.

The researchers also see potential for investigating arginine supplementation in people at elevated risk of respiratory viral infections.

For now, these possibilities remain experimental. The findings do not establish that taking arginine supplements prevents or treats cancer, influenza, or COVID-19 in humans.

Nevertheless, the research reveals an important connection between nutrition and immunity. Rather than simply providing the raw materials needed to build proteins, specific amino acids may help determine how effectively the body's immune defenses identify and respond to dangerous threats.

And because arginine is inexpensive and widely available, the discovery could provide a practical starting point for future studies aimed at strengthening the immune system against cancer and infectious diseases.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 12:19 EST / NOVEMBER 24 2026.

Sources indicate that cloudera Inc. today unveiled a digital sovereignty package that it mentioned enables organizations to maintain control over their data, artificial intelligence models and computing infrastructure regardless of where workloads run.

Industry observers note that cloudera for Digital Sovereignty combines the firm’s Anywhere Cloud, Open Data Lakehouse and Unified Data Fabric technologies with open-weight AI models and model customization tools from Mistral SAS, with whom Cloudera recently partnered. The integrated offering supports deployment across sovereign clouds, private data centers and fully air-gapped environments that have no connection to external networks.

Digital sovereignty is becoming a more pressing concern as enterprises move beyond managing data residency to ensuring that the AI models and infrastructure they depend upon remain under their control. McKinsey & Co. reported last year that 71% of the executives it surveyed called sovereign AI an “existential concern” or “strategic imperative.” Cloudera remarked its own research found that regulation, privacy and data sovereignty requirements rank among the top three barriers to scaling AI.

“As AI becomes more autonomous and embedded in critical operations, enterprises need to know that their data, models, and infrastructure can remain under their control even as technology and regulatory requirements change,” Cloudera Chief Technology Officer Sergio Gago remarked in a statement.

In a recent development, the offering provides consistent zero-trust access controls, data lineage tracking and governance policies across deployment environments. Those capabilities are intended to help organizations address requirements imposed by the European Union’s AI Act, Digital Operational Resilience Act and Network and Information Security Directive, among other regulations.

Governance policies also extend to the enterprise data that AI agents retrieve and use in performing tasks. Mistral’s open-weight models can run alongside governed data, enabling organizations to customize models locally and execute agentic workflows without exposing sensitive information.

Cloudera’s modular hybrid cloud architecture enables customers to shift computing workloads between infrastructure providers and private data centers without rewriting applications or migrating or duplicating underlying data. Organizations can also selectively apply sovereignty controls to sensitive workloads without imposing the same restrictions across their entire computing estate.

According to recent reports, moor Insights & Strategy Inc. #110841. Latest Update: A common osteoporosis drug blocked spinal damage in a surprising newly introduced study

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1486 w)

Latest Update: A common osteoporosis drug blocked spinal damage in a surprising newly introduced study

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1486 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that an existing osteoporosis drug has shown surprising promise in protecting the spine from damage, raising hopes for fresh treatments for chronic neck and back pain.
  • According to recent reports, the discovery could help scientists tackle one of the underlying causes of back pain: the gradual deterioration of the discs that cushion the bones of the spine.
  • Recent findings suggest that although the findings have not yet been confirmed in humans, they suggest that medications already used for other conditions could offer fresh ways to slow spinal degeneration.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that an existing osteoporosis drug has shown surprising promise in protecting the spine from damage, raising hopes for fresh treatments for chronic neck and back pain. In experiments involving zebrafish, researchers found that the medication prevented abnormal mineral deposits from forming in the spine, a process that can cause spinal tissues to harden and vertebrae to fuse together.

According to recent reports, the discovery could help scientists tackle one of the underlying causes of back pain: the gradual deterioration of the discs that cushion the bones of the spine. Researchers also identified changes in gene activity and metabolism that appear to contribute to this damage, revealing several possible targets for future treatments.

Recent findings suggest that although the findings have not yet been confirmed in humans, they suggest that medications already used for other conditions could offer fresh ways to slow spinal degeneration. The research also demonstrates how zebrafish could help scientists investigate the causes of spinal disease and test potential therapies.

Sources indicate that most people experience back pain at some point in their lives, and one common cause is the deterioration of the spine's natural shock absorbers. These structures, called intervertebral discs, sit between the vertebrae and help the spine absorb pressure, distribute weight, and move comfortably.

Over time, the discs can lose their ability to cushion the spine, a condition known as intervertebral disc degeneration (IVDD). As the discs deteriorate, they can contribute to pain, stiffness, and reduced mobility.

Despite the widespread impact and substantial economic burden of this condition, no medications are currently available that can stop or reverse the degenerative process. Surgery remains the only established long-term intervention for certain severe cases, creating an urgent need for treatments that address the underlying damage.

According to recent reports, researchers have long known that genetics influences the risk of developing spinal disc degeneration. One gene of particular interest is associated with collagen IX, a protein that helps maintain the structural integrity of spinal discs by supporting the network of fibers that holds them together. Variations affecting this gene have repeatedly been associated with disc problems that develop earlier in life.

To investigate how these genetic changes contribute to spinal damage, scientists at the Universities of Edinburgh and Bristol turned to zebrafish. They studied fish that had been bred without a functioning copy of the gene, allowing them to observe how its absence affected the spine as the animals grew older.

A Hidden Process Causes the Spine To Harden.

The results revealed striking similarities between the genetically altered zebrafish and people with degenerative spinal disease.

It has been revealed that as the fish aged, abnormal mineral deposits accumulated in the tissues separating their vertebrae. This process, known as mineralization, involves minerals collecting in tissues where they do not normally belong. In the spine, the buildup can cause normally flexible structures to become unusually rigid, much like unwanted bone forming in the wrong location.

The researchers also observed spinal fusion, in which neighboring vertebrae become joined together. Such changes can interfere with the spine's normal flexibility and movement.

Importantly, the scientists discovered that the damage began well before the mineral deposits appeared. An underlying layer that provides structural support during spinal development started to break down first, suggesting that deterioration of this protective framework may set the stage for later hardening.

This finding could help explain how genetic changes initiate a chain reaction that eventually damages the spine.

Surprising Links to Fat Metabolism and Vitamin A.

Sources indicate that to understand what was happening at the molecular level, the team examined patterns of gene activity in the zebrafish. This allowed them to identify biological processes that had become unusually active or disrupted as spinal degeneration developed.

Several unexpected connections emerged.

The researchers found alterations in fat metabolism, the processes through which the body breaks down, stores, and uses fats. They also detected disturbances in a cellular signaling system called mTOR, which helps regulate cell growth, metabolism, and responses to nutrients.

It has been revealed that additional changes involved phosphate regulation and vitamin A signaling. Phosphate is an essential mineral involved in building bones and teeth, but its accumulation in the wrong tissues can contribute to abnormal hardening. Vitamin A signaling helps control how cells develop and function.

Recent findings suggest that together, these findings suggest that spinal disc degeneration involves more than the gradual wearing down of tissues. Changes in how cells process nutrients, regulate growth, and handle minerals may also play important roles.

An Osteoporosis Drug Blocks Spinal Mineral Buildup.

One of the most promising discoveries came when researchers tested ways to reduce the spinal abnormalities.

A medication belonging to a class of drugs called bisphosphonates successfully blocked the abnormal mineral buildup in the zebrafish. Bisphosphonates are already used to treat osteoporosis, a condition in which bones become weaker and more vulnerable to fractures. These medications help protect bones by slowing the processes that break down bone tissue.

The finding is especially intriguing because it suggests that a treatment already used in patients might also help researchers develop therapies for spinal degeneration.

Recent findings suggest that the team identified other approaches that reduced spinal damage. Limiting how much food the zebrafish consumed led to fewer spinal fusions, as did medications that suppressed fat metabolism.

These results point toward fat metabolism and phosphate regulation as potentially vital targets for future drugs.

Recent findings suggest that however, the experiments were conducted in zebrafish, not humans. More research will be needed to determine whether the same biological mechanisms operate in people and whether targeting them can safely prevent or slow spinal disc degeneration. The dietary findings also do not establish that restricting food intake can prevent spinal damage in humans.

Newly introduced Hope for Chronic Back Pain Treatments.

The study was published in the journal Communications Biology and received support from Arthritis UK and BBSRC.

In a recent development, dr. Erika Kague, who led the research at the University of Edinburgh's Institute of Genetics and Cancer, emphasized the potential significance of identifying treatments that target the underlying causes of spinal damage.

"For decades, surgery has been the only real answer for disc disease. By understanding the biology that drives the spine to harden, our zebrafish studies point to several ways of slowing it down, including a drug already used safely in patients. There's more work to do, but for a condition that's affected people for generations without a treatment in sight, this is super exciting.".

The findings could be particularly vital for the millions of people who live with persistent back pain and have limited options for preventing their condition from worsening.

Dr. Caroline Aylott, Head of Research Delivery at Arthritis UK, highlighted the potential benefits for patients.

"For the 9.5 million people across the UK living with back pain this research brings fresh hope that potential fresh therapeutic approaches are on the horizon.

Industry observers note that "We are proud to fund research that is unlocking the science behind the processes leading to spinal disc degeneration. Back pain is one of the UK's most common conditions that has blighted millions over generations. Dr. Erika Kague and her team at the University of Edinburgh have uncovered important genetic evidence that could pave the way for latest treatments, bringing us one step closer to a future where fewer people have to live with the daily pain and challenges that back pain can bring.".

The research also illustrates the broader value of studying basic biological processes to understand diseases that affect large numbers of people.

Dr. Jef Grainger, Executive Director for Bioscience Advancing Knowledge at BBSRC, stated:.

Sources indicate that "This research demonstrates how publicly funded discovery bioscience can generate the knowledge needed to address major health challenges. By revealing new knowledge of how healthy biological processes break down in aging-related spinal disc degeneration, the study opens up promising avenues for future treatment development. It's a great example of how BBSRC-supported research helps turn scientific discovery into knowledge and innovations that have the potential to improve people's lives.".

By identifying genetic and metabolic changes that contribute to spinal hardening, and demonstrating that some of the damage can be prevented in zebrafish, the researchers have opened several new avenues for investigating spinal disc degeneration.

For a condition that affects millions and has no approved drug capable of stopping its progression, these early findings offer an encouraging starting point for developing treatments that could one day protect the spine before serious damage occurs.

CMS to withdraw moratorium on new ACA broker registrations" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

According to recent reports, UPDATED: Nov 20 at 1:30 p.m. ET.

The Trump administration has agreed to withdraw its moratorium on newly introduced broker enrollments, court documents show.

Recent findings suggest that according to a filing submitted Thursday, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Service will published a withdrawal on the Federal Register. The move follows a court ruling earlier this month in favor of two leading organizations representing brokers, which granted a preliminary injunction on the moratorium.

According to recent reports, the National Association of Benefits and Insurance Professionals and Health Agents for America both sued over the regulation. NABIP argued that the moratorium would have a significant impact on licensed professionals operating in accordance with the law.

Per the document, that stay will remain in place until CMS publishes its withdrawal notice. Once that has been put forth, the plaintiffs will dismiss their complaints as moot. CMS also agreed not to take further action against agents and brokers during the current open enrollment period.

The moratorium, finalized in September, was a part the agency's broader efforts to root out fraud, waste and abuse on the Affordable Care Act's exchanges.

UPDATED: Nov. 5 at 4:30 p.m. ET.

A federal court has granted a preliminary injunction to two key groups representing insurance brokers over the Trump administration's moratorium on latest broker enrollments.

The District Court of Maryland issued the injunction after determining that the National Association of Benefits and Insurance Professionals and Health Agents for America "have shown that they are likely to succeed on the merits of their claims under the Administrative Procedure Act.".

The court also said that the organizations made clear they would likely suffer significant harm if the moratorium stays in place.

It has been revealed that NABIP stated that the ruling means that it will restart training for upcoming brokers beginning on Nov. 6.

"Today’s ruling is a significant victory for licensed agents and brokers and the consumers who rely on their expertise," noted NABIP President Mychal Walker in an announcement (PDF). "With Open Enrollment already underway, every day matters.".

"Lifting the moratorium immediately and beginning training tomorrow will help affected professionals get to work assisting individuals and families in finding coverage that fits their needs and budgets," remarked Walker.

It has been revealed that NABIP initially sued on Oct. 15 to challenge the moratorium. The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services instituted the moratorium in late September as part of its broader push to combat fraud on the Affordable Care Act's exchanges.

Sources indicate that PUBLISHED: Oct. 15 at 5:15 p.m. ET.

The National Association of Benefits and Insurance Professionals is suing the Trump administration over its moratorium on new brokers entering the Affordable Care Act marketplaces.

The organization, the leading trade group for insurance brokers and agents, said the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services' moratorium impacts close to 19,000 brokers and agents who will be barred from registering ahead of open enrollment.

Sources indicate that CMS unveiled the moratorium in late September as part of its ongoing push to root out fraud, waste and abuse. In addition, the agency stated it would terminate more than 200 agents and brokers that failed to comply with marketplace standards.

The agency stated newly introduced brokers and agents were disproportionately responsible for submitting inappropriate enrollments and engaging in behaviors at high risk for fraud.

In an announcement (PDF), NABIP notes that it supports the broader effort to combat fraud, but that CMS' moratorium "threatens the livelihoods of thousands of legitimate, licensed professionals who have not been accused of fraud and limits consumers’ access to professional assistance as they navigate Open Enrollment.".

The organization argues in the lawsuit that the rule instituting the moratorium violates both the Administrative Procedure Act and the Affordable Care Act. The regulation is unlawful as it is "arbitrary, capricious, and unsupported by sufficient evidence," NABIP stated.

The 19,000 agents who would be barred from participating under the rule are part of a critical network of professionals who help consumers find coverage that meets their needs, the organization said.

NABIP President Mychal Walker noted that CMS should look elsewhere in its fraud efforts.

Industry observers note that "The existence of fraud is not in dispute. NABIP has raised these concerns with CMS repeatedly and has offered concrete solutions to address them," Walker noted in the announcement. "What is in dispute is whether the appropriate response is to exclude thousands of legitimate agents based solely on whether they registered last year, without any individualized evidence about them.".

"There is a better approach: target fraud where it occurs, strengthen the system’s security and hold bad actors accountable while preserving consumers’ access to trusted professionals," Walker continued.

CMS has taken steps to crack down on brokers as the agency views improper ACA enrollments as a key target in its fight against fraud. CMS officials have repeatedly raised concerns that people are enrolled in ACA looks without their knowledge, or despite being deceased.

Earlier this week, the agency revealed it will purge 189,000 enrollees who are at the moment listed as enrolled in both ACA looks and other coverage, such as Medicaid or Medicare.

#110836. Latest Update: Alzheimer’s may start shrinking two brain regions years before memory loss

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1133 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: Alzheimer’s may start shrinking two brain regions years before memory loss

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1133 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that alzheimer's disease may begin leaving detectable clues in the brain as much as a decade before memory problems appear.
  • The discovery could eventually help doctors recognize Alzheimer's years before symptoms develop, potentially allowing treatment to begin when it has the greatest chance of protecting the brain.
  • Recent findings suggest that by examining hundreds of brain scans, the scientists found that the entorhinal cortex and amygdala, two regions involved in memory and emotion, begin losing tissue earlier than the hippocampus.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that alzheimer's disease may begin leaving detectable clues in the brain as much as a decade before memory problems appear. Researchers at Johns Hopkins University have identified two brain regions that show signs of deterioration earlier than the hippocampus, the area commonly examined for evidence of the disease.

The discovery could eventually help doctors recognize Alzheimer's years before symptoms develop, potentially allowing treatment to begin when it has the greatest chance of protecting the brain.

Recent findings suggest that by examining hundreds of brain scans, the scientists found that the entorhinal cortex and amygdala, two regions involved in memory and emotion, begin losing tissue earlier than the hippocampus. These changes may offer important new clues about how Alzheimer's develops and how it could be detected before significant cognitive decline occurs.

"We have found that there are early changes in the brain manifesting the clinical biomarkers of atrophy as much as a decade before there are clinical symptoms," stated biomedical engineer and senior author Michael Miller. "It's at least a 5-to-10-year play where your brain is changing. Imagine if we could start to treat the neurodegenerative changes at the 2, 3 or 4-year point rather than after 15 years when the changes are manifesting in memory symptoms. That's the great promise here for your loved ones who are at risk.".

The findings were recently published in NeuroImage Reports and are being presented at Neuroscience 2026, the annual meeting of the Society for Neuroscience.

Detecting Alzheimer's Before Memory Loss Begins.

Alzheimer's is the most common cause of dementia worldwide, but the disease does not begin when someone first experiences forgetfulness or confusion. Changes associated with Alzheimer's can accumulate in the brain for decades before noticeable symptoms emerge.

Scientists believe this long period of silent progression may provide a crucial opportunity for treatment. Interventions that begin before extensive damage occurs could potentially do more to preserve memory and other cognitive abilities. However, taking advantage of that opportunity requires reliable ways to identify the disease in its earliest stages.

Sources indicate that one promising approach involves biomarkers, measurable biological changes that can indicate the presence or progression of a disease. In Alzheimer's research, these markers could help reveal who is developing the condition before symptoms become apparent.

"Our goal is to be able to treat individuals before the symptoms of Alzheimer's disease develop so that they may delayed or even stopped," said Marilyn Albert, co-author and director of the Johns Hopkins Alzheimer's Disease Research Center.

Two Brain Regions Reveal Earlier Warning Signs.

To investigate where the earliest detectable changes occur, the researchers examined hundreds of magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and positron emission tomography (PET) scans collected through two independent research projects: the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative and the Biomarkers of Cognitive Decline Among Normal Individuals study.

The scans followed people at different stages of Alzheimer's disease over time, including individuals without symptoms, those experiencing cognitive impairment, and patients who ultimately died from the disease.

Recent findings suggest that in both groups, the researchers observed a consistent pattern. The entorhinal cortex and amygdala, which are located near the hippocampus, indicated greater relative tissue loss during the early stages of Alzheimer's than the hippocampus itself.

This distinction matters because the hippocampus plays a central role in memory and has traditionally been a major focus when doctors look for Alzheimer's-related brain damage.

Industry observers note that the two newly highlighted regions perform important functions of their own. The entorhinal cortex helps retrieve previously stored memories, while the amygdala contributes to emotional memory, including how emotional experiences are processed and remembered.

Their earlier shrinkage suggests that examining these structures together could reveal signs of Alzheimer's that might be less apparent when attention is focused primarily on the hippocampus.

Brain Shrinkage Linked to Alzheimer's Tau Protein.

The researchers also found an important connection between the loss of brain tissue and tau, a protein closely associated with Alzheimer's disease.

According to recent reports, under normal conditions, tau helps maintain the internal structure of nerve cells. In Alzheimer's, however, tau can accumulate abnormally and form tangles that interfere with healthy brain function.

Recent findings suggest that using PET imaging and digital pathology, the scientists found that areas of gray matter shrinkage overlapped with regions showing tau-related changes. Gray matter contains large numbers of nerve cell bodies and is essential for processing information throughout the brain.

This relationship strengthens the possibility that changes in the entorhinal cortex and amygdala could serve as useful indicators of early Alzheimer's disease.

The team believes that measuring tissue loss in both regions, rather than relying primarily on changes in the hippocampus, could eventually improve predictions of who is likely to develop cognitive decline.

According to recent reports, as brain imaging becomes more accessible and less expensive, this approach could also become increasingly practical. For people with a family history of Alzheimer's or other risk factors, researchers envision a future in which doctors might examine these regions as early as a person's 30s or 40s.

"As biomarkers and treatments become increasingly available, knowing who is going to have cognitive decline is going to be really vital," said co-author Meaghan Morris, a neuropathologist who studies Alzheimer's and other dementias. "This could really play into better risk stratification for identifying who is going to have cognitive decline in the near future -- and treating people earlier and earlier to hopefully slow the course of the disease.".

A Potential New Path Toward Earlier Alzheimer's Treatment.

Although the findings are promising, more research is necessary before doctors can use these brain changes as a reliable diagnostic tool. The study identifies potential early biomarkers, but it does not yet establish a clinical test capable of predicting Alzheimer's years in advance.

Recent findings suggest that the next step is to investigate what happens within these regions at a much smaller scale. The researchers want to understand the molecular changes surrounding abnormal tau accumulation and how those changes contribute to the progressive loss of brain tissue.

Identifying the biological processes involved could eventually reveal new targets for therapies designed to interrupt Alzheimer's before extensive damage occurs.

Industry observers note that "Our future work is to better show the molecular neighborhoods associated with these Tau protein changes as localized by these clinical biomarkers of atrophy," Miller noted. "Once we know more about the molecular neighborhoods, we can develop therapies.".

Materials provided by Johns Hopkins University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

UnitedHealth Group is joining the ranks of insurers that are suing the feds over the 2027 Medicare Advantage star ratings calculations.

Industry observers note that much like other recent lawsuits, the healthcare giant argues that the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services inappropriately used multiple measures in the calculations. Over the summer, a Georgia federal court sided with MA proposal Clover Health, and tossed 20 measures that were used in its 2026 scores.

That legal ruling has been the basis of much of the current round of legal wrangling.

UnitedHealth remarked in its complaint that it is bringing the lawsuit to ensure "that their 2027 Star Ratings are calculated in accordance with CMS’s statutory authority and procedural obligations.".

Sources indicate that the star ratings are tied to quality bonus payments for Medicare Advantage aims and listed on the Medicare proposal finder to help individuals identify high-quality coverage. When those payments are lower due to a decline in scores, the insurer may not be as nimble in lowering premiums or enhancing benefits.

"The Star Ratings carry real consequences," UnitedHealth wrote in the complaint. "A strategy’s Star Rating thus directly affects the benefits and healthcare offerings that Medicare beneficiaries receive.".

Sources indicate that UPDATED: Nov. 9 at 2:30 p.m. ET.

Elevance Health is the latest insurer to sue the feds over its performance in the latest round of star ratings for the Medicare Advantage program.

The company sued the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services in District of Columbia federal court on Friday, arguing that the 2027 star ratings calculations violated the Administrative Procedure Act in using 11 measures that it says were adopted unlawfully.

In the lawsuit, the firm noted that the harm from including these measures is "concrete and substantial." If they were excluded, it would increase the scores for 12 of its Medicare Advantage contracts and generate $516 million in additional quality bonus payments.

Recent findings suggest that "Their inclusion therefore does more than violate statutory requirements in the abstract: it depresses Elevance Health’s ratings and reduces the funding available for the following payment year," per the lawsuit. "That funding could support broader supplemental benefits, lower premiums and cost-sharing, and improved care coordination.".

"CMS’s unlawful methodology puts those resources out of reach," the tech giant said.

In a recent development, in addition to the financial impacts, Elevance argues that the star ratings scores can also lead to reputational damage that makes it harder for them to compete in the MA market. It also provides prospective enrollees with inaccurate information, the company noted.

"Beneficiaries cannot make informed coverage choices when the government’s own comparison tool conveys a distorted assessment of the plans available to them," Elevance mentioned.

According to recent reports, "An artificially depressed rating does not merely place Elevance Health at a competitive disadvantage; it undermines the very comparison the program is supposed to enable," the manufacturer continued. "A rating lowered by unlawful measures presents beneficiaries with a misleading signal of relative quality, rather than a lawful basis for distinguishing among competing plans.".

According to recent reports, UPDATED: Oct. 27 at 2:45 p.m. ET.

CVS Heath's Aetna is joining the ranks of insurers suing over its results in the 2027 Medicare Advantage star ratings.

The insured filed suit Monday in Georgia's Southern District Court, and argues that 28 measures used by the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services to calculate its scores were "unlawfully adopted" and should have been excluded.

In a recent development, the court is the same venue that ruled in favor of Clover Health over the summer, and set aside 20 measures that were used to determine its 2026 scores. That decision, which the feds have appealed, kicked off a broad recalculation of 2026 scores that looked different for insurers outside of Clover, triggering a wave of litigation.

In its lawsuit, Aetna cites the Clover decision in finding that CMS extended beyond its statutory authority in deploying those 20 measures.

The organization remarked that calculating its scores using the 28 measures in question will likely cost it $2 billion in 2028 quality bonus payments and rebate retention. Those are funds that the insurer could "apply toward expanding member benefits, reducing premiums and investing in quality improvement.".

Aetna adds that in addition to the monetary loss, having lower scores negatively impacts the company's reputation and its ability to attract potential members.

According to recent reports, "The harm to CVS Health is not exclusively financial; lower ratings carry meaningful reputational harm, which can in turn impact membership," per the lawsuit. "By incorporating unlawful measures into the 2027 Star Ratings calculation, CMS cast CVS Health’s ratings in a poorer light in the eyes of Medicare Advantage consumers relative to peer MAOs, undermining CVS Health’s ability to compete for Medicare beneficiaries through enhanced benefits and the like.".

Aetna did not respond to a request for comment at the time of publication.

In a recent development, based on an analysis from Stephens, 69% of Aetna's MA members are in intends with four or more stars for 2027, down from 81%. That threshold is the key to securing quality bonus payments.

Aetna's complaint follows others focused on the 2027 scores from Centene and Alignment Healthcare (see those stories below).

Centene has become the latest insurer to sue the federal government over its 2027 Medicare Advantage star ratings.

In a lawsuit filed Thursday in Georgia's Southern District Court, the company argues that the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services violated the Administrative Procedure Act in determining its latest scores. Centene says that CMS ran afoul of "core statutory safeguards" in deploying 17 measures.

The use of those measures ultimately caused "significant injury" to the firm, according to the complaint. For 2027, 9% of Centene's members are enrolled in plans with at least four stars, which declined from 18% in the prior year.

"In implementing each of the individual Star measures that Centene challenges, CMS violated applicable law and thereby caused Centene to lose out on hundreds of millions of dollars in revenue that Centene could use to strengthen benefits, reduce premiums, and improve health outcomes," the organization remarked in the lawsuit.

It has been revealed that CMS argues that the court has already sided with a similar argument in its decision in favor of Clover Health earlier this year. In that case, which led to a broad recalculation in scores, the courts set aside 20 measures that were used in determining Clover's star ratings for 2026.

If the 17 measures in question had been excluded in calculating Centene's scores, the company estimates it would receive $448 million more in quality bonus payments for the 2028 strategy year, funds it would deploy to expand benefits, lower premiums and enhance programs like care coordination.

In addition to the financial impact, a drop in star ratings also carries a reputational hit, Centene said.

"Beyond the financial impact to the organization and its members, depressed ratings also inflict significant reputational damage and diminished membership," the company stated in the complaint.

Centene had not returned a request for comment at the time of publication.

According to recent reports, PUBLISHED: Oct. 12 at 3 p.m. ET.

Alignment Healthcare sued federal regulators, alleging that its 2027 Medicare Advantage star ratings were determined "in flagrant violation" of statute.

In the lawsuit filed Friday in District of Columbia federal court, the insurer says that the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services "has completely departed from Congress’s vision of leveraging predictable, valid measures developed with input from providers, intends, and the public" in establishing the methodology for the star ratings.

The manufacturer argues that rather than establish "consistent, stable specifications" for metrics through the traditional rule-making process, the agency instead detailed key measures through a series of "technical notes." This violates the Administrative Procedure Act, per the lawsuit.

The program's star ratings are the critical determinant in quality bonus payments to insurers as well as a tool that aims to make it easier for enrollees and brokers to identify benefits with the highest quality.

"Consistent application of the statutory requirements governing Star Ratings is therefore essential not only to proposal payments and competition but also to ensuring that beneficiaries can rely on the Star Ratings as meaningful and comparable measures of plan quality," Alignment noted in the lawsuit.

In a recent development, the company adds that multiple recent court decisions have set aside CMS' star ratings methodology, notably a ruling over the summer in favor of Clover Health that tossed 20 metrics used in the 2026 calculations. A Georgia federal judge determined that 10 measures utilized exceeded CMS' authority, while 10 other measures were promulgated inappropriately.

CMS recalculated the scores across the board following the ruling, but only set aside the 10 measures that the courts determined were outside the bounds of its regulatory authority. The agency maintained that approach in the 2027 calculations, Alignment argues.

"Congress created the Star Ratings program to allow Medicare Advantage beneficiaries to make informed decisions about blueprint enrollment based on clinically validated measures of plan quality that had been subjected to notice and comment," the manufacturer mentioned. "CMS’s contrary approach fails to carry out the vision that Congress set forth by statute.".

The Trump administration has appealed the Clover decision, so that legal case remains ongoing.

In addition, Alignment argues it suffered reputational and financial damage as a result of its 2027 scores, which plummeted compared to the prior year. Just 25% of its members are in looks with four or more stars for 2027, down from 100% in 2026.

Shares in the firm tumbled following the release of the ratings, though stock prices have rebounded since.

Alignment sued the feds following the Clover decision to secure a recalculation for its scores that aligns with the court's decision, and in a statement to Fierce Healthcare, said that the lawsuit aligns with that perspective.

In a recent development, "Our lawsuit seeks to ensure that the Star Ratings program operates as Congress intended and that Alignment is properly compensated for the care we provide," Alignment mentioned in the statement. "We respect the judicial process and will present our case in court. Because this matter involves pending litigation, we will not comment on the specific legal arguments beyond our filings.".

"Our focus remains on delivering exceptional care, improving health outcomes and advocating for a stable, lawful regulatory framework that supports seniors and strengthens the Medicare Advantage program," the organization said.

#110832. Breaking: MIT discovers that aging weakens the brain’s nighttime cleaning system
