Breaking: MIT discovers that aging weakens the brain’s nighttime cleaning system

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1678 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • While we sleep, the brain carries out an essential maintenance process that helps wash away accumulated waste.
  • Recent findings suggest that researchers discovered that waves of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), which help carry waste out of the brain, are significantly weaker in older adults.
  • The findings raise key questions about whether weakened brain cleansing could contribute to Alzheimer's disease and other forms of dementia.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

While we sleep, the brain carries out an essential maintenance process that helps wash away accumulated waste. But new research from MIT suggests that this natural cleaning system becomes less effective as we grow older, revealing another way aging can change the brain beyond simply disrupting sleep.

Recent findings suggest that researchers discovered that waves of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), which help carry waste out of the brain, are significantly weaker in older adults. The decline appears to be connected to changes in the slow electrical waves that occur during deep sleep, as well as changes in how blood moves through the brain. Importantly, the reduced fluid movement cannot be explained simply by older people spending less time asleep.

The findings raise key questions about whether weakened brain cleansing could contribute to Alzheimer's disease and other forms of dementia. The team now hopes to determine whether changes in these fluid waves could eventually help identify people at greater risk of cognitive decline.

"We know that people age really differently. Some people age very successfully with great cognitive outcomes, and other people develop cognitive decline. If we can figure out who has great trajectories of aging and what are the factors that are associated with that, we might be able to use that to predict future outcomes," notes Laura Lewis, the Athinoula A. Martinos Associate Professor of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science, a member of MIT's Institute for Medical Engineering and Science and the Research Laboratory of Electronics, and an associate member of the Picower Institute for Learning and Memory.

Lewis and her colleagues also want to investigate whether treatments or other interventions could strengthen this waste-clearing process in older adults.

The study was published in Nature Aging, with Lewis serving as senior author. Its lead authors are Sydney Bailes, a postdoctoral researcher in MIT's Laboratory for Information and Decision Systems, and Stephanie Williams, a former MIT visiting student who received her PhD from Boston University in 2026.

How Deep Sleep Helps the Brain Clear Waste.

Deep sleep does much more than leave us feeling refreshed. During its deepest stages, known as non-REM sleep, the brain produces powerful, slow electrical waves that support physical recovery, strengthen memories, and help regulate other essential functions.

Sources indicate that in 2019, Lewis and her colleagues discovered that these slow brain waves also help generate rhythmic movements of cerebrospinal fluid. The fluid moves through spaces around the brain and plays an crucial role in carrying away waste products.

In a recent development, that earlier discovery led to a fresh question. Because slow brain waves typically weaken with age, could the fluid movements responsible for clearing waste also become less effective?

Previous research had produced conflicting results. Some studies suggested that cerebrospinal fluid movement declined with age, while others reported increases. However, those investigations had not directly monitored the fluid during sleep, when the brain's natural cleaning activity is especially crucial.

To investigate, the MIT team recruited two groups of volunteers. Younger participants were between 18 and 39 years old, while the older group ranged from 60 to 84.

Each volunteer completed a testing session lasting approximately two hours. The sessions began late at night, increasing the likelihood that participants would become sleepy during the measurements.

The researchers combined several techniques to observe what was happening inside the brain. Functional magnetic resonance imaging, or fMRI, allowed them to track changes in cerebral blood flow. A specialized MRI method developed by Lewis measured cerebrospinal fluid movement, while electroencephalography, or EEG, recorded the brain's electrical activity.

Many participants fell asleep inside the scanner, providing an opportunity to compare their brain activity and fluid movements during wakefulness and sleep.

The results revealed a striking age difference. As younger adults entered non-REM sleep, their slow brain waves grew stronger and were accompanied by larger waves of cerebrospinal fluid. In older adults, however, the average fluid waves were substantially smaller.

The findings indicated that aging was associated with a weakening of the fluid movements that normally accompany deep sleep.

Why the Aging Brain's Cleaning Waves Weaken.

The researchers next investigated what might be causing this decline. In a separate set of experiments conducted while participants were fully awake, they examined how the brain's blood vessels responded to different demands.

One possible explanation involved neurovascular coupling, the process that connects brain activity with blood flow.

According to recent reports, when a particular region of the brain becomes more active, its cells require additional oxygen and nutrients. Nearby blood vessels normally widen to deliver more blood, ensuring that the active cells receive the resources they need.

In a recent development, to measure this response, the researchers indicated volunteers a flickering checkerboard pattern while monitoring blood flow with fMRI. The rapidly changing visual pattern stimulates activity in regions involved in processing vision, which should trigger an increase in local blood supply.

According to recent reports, in many older participants, the brain's electrical activity increased as expected, but the corresponding rise in blood flow was much smaller. This suggested that aging had weakened the ability of blood vessels to respond to the brain's changing oxygen requirements.

The team then performed a second experiment to examine the brain's broader vascular responsiveness.

It has been revealed that participants were instructed to hold their breath while researchers monitored changes in cerebral blood flow. Holding one's breath causes carbon dioxide to accumulate in the bloodstream, which normally prompts blood vessels in the brain to widen and increase blood flow.

Once again, the older group showed a weaker response. On average, their cerebral blood flow increased less than it did in younger volunteers.

Together, these experiments indicated that changes in the brain's vascular system could help explain why its waste-clearing fluid waves diminish with age.

In a recent development, using a statistical model, the scientists found that weakened neurovascular coupling and reduced blood flow responses accounted for much of the decline in cerebrospinal fluid movement. However, the two mechanisms did not explain the entire difference, suggesting that additional biological changes associated with aging are also involved.

"Aging is so complex, and so many different things change, that it's really hard to disentangle the individual factors," Bailes claims. "We try to account for some of the mechanisms, but there definitely are a lot of other factors related to vascular health and lifestyle. If you were able to measure all of them, you might be able to break it apart into different explanations for why an individual's CSF flow might be more or less impaired.".

Could Weaker Brain Cleansing Increase Dementia Risk?

The discovery may have vital implications for understanding neurological diseases associated with aging.

Earlier studies have linked disrupted sleep to a greater risk of Alzheimer's disease and other forms of dementia. Because cerebrospinal fluid helps remove waste from the brain, researchers are particularly interested in whether age-related changes in its movement might contribute to neurodegeneration.

According to recent reports, none of the volunteers in the MIT study had been diagnosed with a neurodegenerative disorder. However, brain scans revealed that some older participants demonstrated signs of gray matter atrophy, meaning a loss of brain tissue in regions containing large numbers of nerve cells.

Those changes were associated with greater reductions in cerebrospinal fluid movement.

It has been revealed that the relationship does not establish that weakened fluid flow causes brain tissue loss or dementia. Nevertheless, it provides a reason to investigate whether these changes might serve as early warning signs of neurological decline.

The researchers hope to follow some of the participants over time to determine whether reduced cerebrospinal fluid movement is associated with a greater likelihood of developing a neurodegenerative condition.

Can the Brain's Nighttime Cleaning System Be Restored?

Beyond understanding why brain cleansing declines, the MIT team is exploring whether it might be possible to improve the process.

One promising possibility involves sound stimulation during sleep.

It has been revealed that in a separate recent study, Lewis' laboratory found that brief bursts of "pink noise" could increase cerebrospinal fluid movement in younger adults. Pink noise is a type of sound that contains a broad range of frequencies, with greater emphasis on lower frequencies than white noise.

Although the approach has shown potential in younger people, researchers have not yet tested whether it can produce similar effects in older adults.

Another intriguing finding could provide clues about how to preserve the brain's natural cleaning abilities.

Sources indicate that while older participants generally had weaker cerebrospinal fluid waves than younger adults, the decline was not universal. Some older volunteers retained fluid movements that were comparable to those measured in healthy younger people.

This raises the possibility that certain biological or lifestyle factors may help protect the brain's waste-removal system against aging.

According to recent reports, "It's really intriguing that for some of these older adults, their CSF fell right in the range of the healthy young adults," Lewis indicates. "We are really interested in what's different in those people and how that might be related to future health outcomes.".

Understanding why some older brains maintain these youthful fluid movements could ultimately help researchers identify ways to support healthier brain aging and investigate whether preserving the brain's nighttime cleaning system can reduce the risk of cognitive decline.

The research received funding from the National Institutes of Health, the Simons Collaboration on Plasticity in the Aging Brain, a McKnight Scholar Award, a Pew Biomedical Scholar Award, an MIT EECS Transformative Research Award, the Picower Institute Neurological Disorder Discovery Research Fund, a Sloan Fellowship, and the Department of Defense National Defense Science and Engineering Graduate Fellowship Program.

XRP is having its worst November on record, but one prominent crypto entrepreneur still sees a four-digit price ahead. EasyA co-founder Dom Kwok has reiterated his $1,000 XRP target for 2030, even as the token crashes toward $0.90 and institutional investors pull money from spot exchange-traded funds (ETFs).

XRP has dropped 25% this month, surpassing its previous November record decline in 2019. The token briefly touched $0.862 over the weekend before recovering toward $0.94. It remains below $1, a level XRP has failed to reclaim since November 14.

The timing makes Kwok’s forecast look almost absurd on a chart. Yet the sell-off is now testing a level where historical capitulation, ETF positioning, and XRP’s long-term adoption thesis collide.

Sources indicate that the institutional story has taken a serious hit, with spot XRP ETFs recording $30.76 million in November outflows, marking their third consecutive week of withdrawals. Assets across the funds have slipped from around $1.42 billion at October’s end to below $1 billion.

It has been revealed that november has also produced no daily net inflow for XRP ETFs so far. That is a sharp reversal from the buying streak that helped fuel institutional optimism earlier this year. Still, cumulative net inflows remain near $1.78 billion since launch. Investors have pulled money recently, but the institutional trade has not disappeared.

Right now, XRP’s chart is already showing signs of trying to stabilize. The token has bounced from its weekend low around $0.86, with buyers defending the $0.90 area. The daily Relative Strength Index sits near 32, following its recent oversold dip below 30.

In a recent development, that is not a confirmed reversal. But XRP does not need a massive catalyst to produce a sharp bounce after a decline this aggressive.

LiquidChain is tackling one of crypto’s biggest problems: liquidity scattered across Bitcoin, Ethereum, and Solana. Its Layer 3 network aims to connect these ecosystems through a unified execution environment, allowing developers to build applications accessing multiple networks without deploying separate versions everywhere.

Recent findings suggest that that could unlock cross-chain trading, liquidity pools, and DeFi applications without the usual bridging complexity. Bitcoin brings capital, Ethereum brings DeFi depth, and Solana offers fast execution. LiquidChain wants developers to access all three through one infrastructure layer.

If LiquidChain delivers its unified liquidity vision, it could offer developers a reason to build beyond a single blockchain ecosystem. That is what makes the project worth watching beyond its presale numbers.

Kwok, a former Goldman Sachs analyst and EasyA co-founder, has publicly noted he believes XRP could reach $1,000 by 2030. His thesis centers on institutional adoption, blockchain utility, and the possibility that XRP becomes part of a much larger global payments infrastructure.

That forecast is a long way from today’s price. At $0.94, XRP would need to rise more than 1,000-fold to reach his target. Kwok XRP price prediction is extremely ambitious, but it puts the current price collapse into perspective: Kwok is betting on what XRP could become, rather than what the chart looks like today.

Recent findings suggest that the immediate battle is much less dramatic. XRP needs to hold $0.90–$0.91 before buyers can seriously challenge $0.95. Reclaiming $1, followed by the $1.03 area, would be the first convincing sign that the November downtrend is losing control.

Failure to hold $0.90 could send XRP back toward $0.862, with $0.80 becoming the next downside target.

Historical data offers a mixed warning. XRP’s five worst November performances before this year were all followed by December losses, averaging 10.4%. However, the losses varied widely. December 2018 and 2016 were comparatively mild, while 2019 extended the damage with another 14.8% decline.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes
CMS issues Medicare Advantage proposals aimed at boosting competition" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

The Trump administration has proposed a slew of changes to Medicare Advantage and Part D designed to "revitalize care" in these markets.

For one, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services said late Friday that it will patch application and network adequacy requirements to make it easier for latest entrants. The agency proposed to require organizations to demonstrate network adequacy during their first year in operation, rather than during the application process.

This shift would eliminate a significant barrier for upcoming entrants, driving greater competition in the market.

CMS has also proposed combining three specialty areas in behavioral health—clinical psychology, clinical social work and outpatient behavioral health—into one specialty group for the purposes of network adequacy. The changes will give prepares greater flexibility in building out behavioral health networks.

CMS will also make adjustments that seek to boost competition for special needs looks.

Sources indicate that in addition, the agency said it will make adjustments to the star ratings program, focusing its ratings on 15 measures. The proposed measure set would emphasize "clinical outcomes and patient experience while retaining select process measures in high-priority areas where performance remains low.".

CMS is also aiming to enhancement the calculation methodology that will "raise the bar for achieving high ratings," and thus quality bonus payments.

"People with Medicare should be able to choose coverage based on what matters most to them—quality, affordability and access," noted CMS Administrator Mehmet Oz, M.D., in the announcement. "These proposals are about creating a Medicare Advantage marketplace that rewards better care and better value while empowering beneficiaries with the options and knowledge they need to make informed decisions about their health.".

In a recent development, the proposed rule also includes provisions that align with Department of Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy's Make America Healthy Again agenda by setting a "healthy food" standard that MA aims should follow for supplemental benefits.

The goal, CMS remarked, is to ensure that Medicare dollars are spent on food benefits that align with MAHA.

"Medicare food benefits should pay for nutritious food that helps people improve their health and manage chronic disease," Kennedy noted in the announcement. "This proposal would require those benefits to meet the Dietary Guidelines for Americans while preserving access to foods and nutritional products that providers recommend for patients’ specific medical needs.".

"Under President Trump, we are putting prevention at the center of health care and demanding more from every Medicare dollar," Kennedy remarked.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Recent findings suggest that in recent years, as the world has continued to evolve, the marketplace for real estate investors has evolved with it.
  • Industry observers note that not all real estate investments have to include purchasing actual bricks and mortar in the physical world.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When it comes to exploring enticing investment opportunities, real estate often stands out as an excellent solution for making and growing wealth. No matter how the world around us changes, there will always be a demand for property in attractive areas. This has led countless people to diversify their portfolios over the years, buying rental properties, second homes, and even office spaces.

Recent findings suggest that in recent years, as the world has continued to evolve, the marketplace for real estate investors has evolved with it. Today, people no longer need to buy and flip entire properties to make money. There are numerous tips for getting started and ways you can start your journey into the property world, and some options are actually simpler and more affordable than you might expect. Here are some of the best, most interesting ways to invest in real estate, if you want to avoid the traditional buy and flip strategy.

Industry observers note that not all real estate investments have to include purchasing actual bricks and mortar in the physical world. The digital landscape has evolved drastically in recent years, introducing fresh opportunities for innovative entrepreneurs to make money buying virtual assets. As the concept of the metaverse continues to gain traction, digital real estate is growing increasingly attractive.

With digital real estate, companies purchase a section of the blockchain in a metaverse landscape, where they can build online experiences, or simply store other assets. In 2021, sales on four of the biggest metaverse platforms for real estate reached a whopping $501 million. This indicates learning how to invest in digital real estate could be a worthwhile strategy for any consumer. Not only is it potentially profitable, but the digital real estate also requires less work to manage and maintain than a physical house or property.

Industry observers note that even if you’re not familiar with this form of property-based investing, you probably know the term crowdfunding. Made popular by sites like GoFundMe and Kickstarter, the crowdfunding strategy involves individuals pooling their resources together to fund a product or business. In the real estate world, investors can work together to purchase a property, such as a corporate space, warehouse, or block of flats, reducing the initial cost of a purchase.

The approach allows investors to participate in products that would have been impossible to access in the past because of high capital requirements. Individuals can use this strategy to diversify their portfolios with a variety of different locations and property types. Plus, you’ll earn a passive income through rental profits, and property appreciation.

Another real estate investment strategy gaining increasing attention in recent years is REITs. These are basically investment vehicles responsible for owning and operating income-generating assets, such as rental properties and office blocks. They’re traded on traditional stock exchanges and provide individuals with an opportunity to invest in the market, without directly owning a property or having to manage the investment themselves.

According to recent reports, REITs can come with several attractive features, including regular distributions of dividends, and the ability to explore a range of different sectors. You can even use this strategy to spread your portfolio across industrial, residential, and commercial properties. They’re also a highly liquid investment option, making them appealing to beginners.

Finally, one interesting way to invest in real estate, without buying a physical property outright, is to spend some of your money on shares in PropTech startups. PropTech, or Property Technology startups, are companies focused on developing tools and real estate designed to transform the property landscape. They develop things like property management solutions, smart home technology, and virtual reality applications for tours.

If you already have experience in the world of stocks and shares, investing in a PropTech company could be an excellent way to utilize your existing knowledge and diversify your portfolio. It’s also a chance to get your foot in the door with a company that’s actively disrupting the real estate space, and the market as we know it.

Industry observers note that investing in property has become a much more diverse and versatile opportunity for individuals in recent years. No matter how much money you can afford to spend, or where your expertise lies, you can find plenty of ways to expand your portfolio with disruptive real-estate investment strategies.

An ancient virus may help explain what makes the human brain different

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (976 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that A virus that infected chimpanzees millions of years ago has left behind a genetic legacy that may help explain an notable difference between human and chimpanzee brain development.
  • It has been revealed that the findings, published in Science Advances, reveal how infections from the distant past can leave lasting changes in the genetic makeup of an entire population.
  • It has been revealed that although pandemics are often considered a modern threat, infectious diseases have been spreading through large animal and human populations for millions of years.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that A virus that infected chimpanzees millions of years ago has left behind a genetic legacy that may help explain an notable difference between human and chimpanzee brain development. Researchers at Lund University have discovered that ancient viral DNA embedded in the chimpanzee genome switches off a gene that remains active in humans and appears to play an important role in the developing brain.

It has been revealed that the findings, published in Science Advances, reveal how infections from the distant past can leave lasting changes in the genetic makeup of an entire population. They also offer new clues about how the brains of humans and our closest evolutionary relatives may have developed differently.

It has been revealed that although pandemics are often considered a modern threat, infectious diseases have been spreading through large animal and human populations for millions of years. Some of these ancient infections left traces of viral DNA that continue to influence how genes function today.

Johan Jakobsson, Professor of Molecular Neurogenetics at Lund University, claims the discovery demonstrates how a virus can introduce genetic changes that eventually become widespread throughout a population.

"The virus we investigated specifically affected chimpanzees. Yet humans and chimpanzees have largely the same genetic makeup. That is why it is key to understand the differences in how genes are regulated. Our findings suggest that one gene, LINC00662, plays a significant role in early human brain development," indicates Johan Jakobsson.

How an Ancient Virus Silenced a Brain Development Gene.

At the center of the discovery is a gene called LINC00662. Researchers found that it is active during early human brain development but completely switched off in comparable chimpanzee brain models.

It has been revealed that the difference appears to be caused by a genetic remnant of PTERV1, an ancient virus that infected chimpanzees millions of years ago. PTERV1 belongs to a group known as endogenous retroviruses, which are viruses whose genetic material became incorporated into the DNA of their hosts. Once embedded in the genome, these viral sequences can be inherited by future generations.

Recent findings suggest that over time, PTERV1 produced numerous copies of its genetic material that became scattered across different parts of the chimpanzee genome. Researchers found that these viral sequences are systematically silenced through a process called methylation.

According to recent reports, methylation involves chemical modifications to DNA that help regulate gene activity. It is one of the ways cells control which genetic instructions are used and which remain inactive. In this case, the ancient viral insertion appears to have caused a neighboring gene involved in brain development to be switched off.

Jakobsson states understanding these differences in gene regulation could also provide crucial insights into how genetic activity protects the brain or contributes to damage and disease.

Miniature Brains Reveal a Striking Genetic Difference.

Sources indicate that to investigate the virus's effects, researchers grew miniature brain models called organoids using stem cells from humans and chimpanzees. These three-dimensional structures reproduce certain features of developing brain tissue, allowing scientists to study aspects of early brain development under controlled laboratory conditions.

When the team compared the two types of organoids, the difference was striking. LINC00662 revealed strong activity in the human brain models but was completely inactive in those derived from chimpanzee cells.

"The gene was strongly expressed in the human organoids, but not at all in the chimpanzee organoids," indicates Patricia Gerdes, postdoc in molecular neurogenetics at Lund University.

The researchers then set out to determine whether the ancient viral DNA was directly responsible for this difference.

Using CRISPR-Cas9, a powerful gene editing technology that allows scientists to make targeted changes to DNA, they removed the viral sequence from chimpanzee cells.

The result provided compelling evidence. Once the viral DNA was removed, the previously inactive LINC00662 gene switched back on.

"This demonstrates that it is in fact the viral insertion that is responsible for the gene being switched off in chimpanzees," notes Patricia Gerdes.

New Clues to Human Brain Evolution.

According to recent reports, the team also wanted to understand what LINC00662 actually does in the human brain. To investigate, they used CRISPR to switch off the gene in human brain organoids and examined how other genes responded.

Disabling LINC00662 reduced the activity of genes associated with nerve cell development and the formation of connections between neurons. These processes are essential for establishing the networks that allow the brain to communicate and function.

The results suggest that LINC00662 contributes to key stages of early human brain development, while the ancient viral insertion prevents the gene from functioning in chimpanzees.

It has been revealed that more broadly, the discovery highlights an key principle of evolution. Although humans and chimpanzees share much of their genetic material, differences in how genes are switched on and off can influence how their bodies and brains develop.

The findings suggest that ancient viral infections may have contributed to these differences by altering gene regulation long after the original infections disappeared.

According to recent reports, researchers now proposal to investigate whether other remnants of ancient viruses have similarly influenced brain evolution. They also hope to determine whether these inherited viral sequences may play a role in neurological diseases.

Together, the discoveries raise an intriguing possibility that some of the differences between human and chimpanzee brains may trace back, at least in part, to viruses that infected our evolutionary relatives millions of years ago.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 13:50 EST / NOVEMBER 24 2026.

Australia-based Myriota Pty. Ltd., a global satellite platform for the industrial internet of things, today declared it has raised $40 million in the first portion of its Series C to launch next-generation satellites and accelerate customer adoption across international markets.

Main Sequence Ventures, Hostplus and Australia’s National Reconstruction Fund Corporation co-led the round. Funds SA joined as a upcoming investor. The round raised the company’s total funding to more than $107.5 million, and is expected to close in early 2027.

Founded in 2015, Myriota’s platform makes satellite connectivity commercially viable for large-scale industrial IoT, using the same core technology to track mining equipment and trailers to also monitor fuel tanks, livestock water supplies and off-grid solar.

The company’s platform combines satellite connectivity, low-power devices, field installation tools and fleet management software to support existing infrastructure. The objective is to provide access to communication tools that connect what is in place with turnkey service, so a company can connect devices, machines and smart sensors no matter how remote they are.

“We’re at the beginning of a fundamental shift in industrial IoT,” Chief Executive Ben Cade mentioned. “Industries increasingly rely on data from the field to make decisions about their operations, assets and resources, and as AI moves into the physical world, that data becomes even more essential.”.

The company expanded its platform over the past 12 months with the launch of HyperPulse, a global 5G non-terrestrial network, or NTN, and terrestrial service, and AssetHawk, a rugged, long-life asset tracker designed to make it economical to track industrial objects.

Industry observers note that alongside the expansion, it also grew into new verticals such as industrial fuels. It monitors and tracks fuel deployments across North America and Latin America, with EMEA and Asia Pacific to follow.

Industry observers note that myriota competes in a sector led by established operators such as Iridium Communications Inc., Orbcomm Inc. and Viasat Inc., alongside a growing field of providers pursuing cheaper, standards-based connections for industrial sensors and trackers.

The company said it intends to use the funds to expand its space infrastructure, including developing and launching its next-generation satellites.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

National growth in home values was flat month over month in September as mortgage rates accelerated and inflation continued running hot.

The value of single-family homes as measured by repeat transactions increased 2.1% year over year, same as in August, according to data from the S&P Cotality Case-Shiller Index released on Tuesday.

However, home values fell in real terms for the 16th consecutive month, as September's 3.7% inflation rate outpaced the home value gain by roughly 1.6 percentage points, up from about 1.3 points in August.

"Nominal home prices remain resilient, but inflation is once again widening the gap between nominal and real housing returns," notes Rebecca Kaufman, associate director of commodities at S&P Dow Jones Indices.

Across the 20 cities tracked by the index, Chicago yet again led the U.S. with a 6.9% annual gain. New York City took second place with a year-over-year increase of 5.8%, but Miami emerged as the month's surprise, finishing third with a 4.6% gain.

"Miami’s rise is particularly notable," points out Kaufman. "After moving into fourth place among the 20 cities in July and August, it has now climbed into the top three, a sharp reversal from its comparatively weak performance in 2025.".

On the other side of the spectrum, Seattle recorded the largest annual decline for the fourth consecutivemonth at 1.9%, followed by Denver (-1.0%) and Dallas (-0.9%), reflecting a persistent regional divergence.

Sources indicate that september also revealed a widening gap between seasonal weakness and underlying price momentum. On a nonseasonally adjusted basis, the U.S. National and 10-City Composite Indices fell 0.3% and 0.5% month over month, respectively, while both rose 0.2% after seasonal adjustment.

"That contrast suggests that some of the apparent monthly weakness reflects the normal fall slowdown rather than a broad deterioration in home prices," adds Kaufman.

The latest Case-Shiller release reflects sales closing from July through September, a period when mortgage rates moved higher, with Freddie Mac's 30-year fixed rate averaging 6.54% in July, near 6.7% in August, and 6.86% in September.

Realtor.com® senior economist Anthony Smith notes that the housing market's momentum has lost steam in recent months. Contract activity softened over the same stretch, with pending home sales down 4.7% from a year earlier in August before setting a series record low in September.

In a recent development, "Looking ahead, the rate and demand backdrop has become more challenging since September closed," states Smith. After four weeks of declines, the 30-year fixed rate jumped back to 7.28% as of Nov. 19, pushed higher by hotter-than-expected October inflation and expectations for a Fed rate hike in December.

The median existing-home sales price rose just 0.4% from a year ago in October, while asking prices were down 2.2% and months' supply reached its highest level since 2015.

"If financing costs stay elevated into the winter, the plateau in price growth could give way to renewed softening, particularly in supply-heavy Southern and Western markets," notes Smith.

The Case-Shiller Index reports on a two-month delay and reflects a three-month moving average of home sales prices.

Homes usually go under contract a month or two before they close, so the September report primarily reflects purchase decisions made in late summer.

Although the index's price data is delayed by several months, it is considered one of the best available measures of changing home values, because it is based on repeat transactions on the same properties.

Recent findings suggest that snejana Farberov is a reporter at Realtor.com covering the U.S. housing market and the latest domestic real estate trends. She has worked as a general assignment journalist in New York City and Long Island for 16 years, writing for New York Post, Daily Mail, and News 12. Snejana earned bachelor's degrees in journalism and Italian from St. John's University, followed by a master’s degree from Columbia University School of Journalism.

Photon pharmacy marketplace integrated with ChatGPT for clinicians" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Photon, a prescription infrastructure manufacturer, is now available as a plugin for ChatGPT to streamline prescribing for clinicians within a tool they already use.

Sources indicate that the option is available to eligible U.S. licensed clinicians using ChatGPT for Clinicians (free for verified clinicians) or ChatGPT for Healthcare. Just as clinicians must accept OpenAI’s BAA before sharing protected patient information, they must accept Photon’s BAA to maintain HIPAA compliance when using Photon in ChatGPT. Controlled substances are not supported. The feature is free for clinicians through Dec. 31, 2026.

It has been revealed that the patient experience remains the same through Photon. What is new is where the clinician can write a prescription. Clinicians with a Photon account can draft, review and send prescriptions without leaving ChatGPT. They just need to add the Photon plugin into ChatGPT, and then they can draft prescriptions. A patient will get a text to Photon’s prescription marketplace outside of ChatGPT. Patients can compare prices and request to change a pharmacy as needed.

“AI is moving from note-taking and reference into treatment workflows. Clinicians are already using ChatGPT to understand treatment options. Once they’ve decided what to prescribe, they should be able to act on that decision in the same conversation,” Otto Sipe, co-founder and CEO, wrote to Fierce Healthcare in an emailed comment. “Photon provides the infrastructure behind that step.”.

In the new interface, clinicians begin a prompt with the name of the patient and medication. Photon uses authorized patient information and treatment context shared with ChatGPT to help prepare a prescription for a clinician’s review. They can also add new patient details during the process. Once saved in Photon, that patient can be found by name for future prescriptions.

From there, clinicians review the prescribing details, including the dosing, instructions and quantity. Clinicians can ask about dosing options in the chat. Patient records are saved in Photon, and draft prescriptions are checked against the patient’s recorded allergies and medications. Finally, clinicians review and authorize the prescription to be sent, remaining responsible for the treatment. Clinicians can check a prescription’s status in ChatGPT.

Ann Michael Maye has given the Christmas tree she shares with her husband, Fresh England Patriots quarterback Drake Maye, a team dress code this year—and even the presents are in red and blue.

Ahead of Thanksgiving, Ann Michael teamed up with Minted to reveal a holiday display that draws as much from her kitchen and her mahjong nights with fellow Patriots wives and girlfriends as it does from the football field.

Photos from the collaboration offer a peek at the finished tree, the couple’s Christmas card, and a fireside game setup with a seat saved for the hostess.

Industry observers note that the tree occupies a sunny corner framed on two sides by tall, white-trimmed windows. It rises nearly to the crown molding, where a scarlet bow sends two wide ribbon tails cascading over the upper branches.

Industry observers note that A blue-and-white patterned armchair sits off to one side. On the other, the gifts have claimed the floor all the way to the window.

In a recent development, in one photo, Ann Michael reaches up to hang a clear ornament bearing a white No. 10, the same number Drake wears on the field. She’s dressed for the occasion in a striped sweater that picks up the reds and blues of the tree, a long brown skirt, and pointed black heels.

A closer view reveals at least two more numbered ornaments, including a 14 and a 74.

Some of the most personal decorations are easy to miss in a wide shot. Small rectangular frames hang vertically from pale ribbons, their blue-and-white borders standing out among the round ornaments.

Each holds a photograph from the past year. In one, two women pose with their arms around each other. Farther up the tree, another group photo is nestled just beneath a gold ornament.

According to recent reports, ann Michael also found room for a miniature version of her “Bakemas” kitchen. Glass cream puffs with ridges of golden pastry and white filling hang alongside embroidered gingerbread figures and a felt stand mixer.

In one close-up, a tiny cupcake with colorful sprinkles peeks out from a branch just below one of the photo frames.

According to recent reports, even the wrapping rewards a closer look. The boxes beneath the tree are covered in deep blue Minted paper with a small repeating pattern.

In a recent development, some are tied with wide red bows that echo the tree topper, while others have navy or silvery blue ribbons. Personalized tags hang from the packages, several of which are stacked two high beneath the lowest branches.

In a recent development, the couple saved a different color combination for their Christmas card. In another photo, Ann Michael holds up a red-and-green plaid design featuring an outdoor portrait of her and Drake.

A white border leaves just enough space beneath the picture for a simple “Merry Christmas.”.

One ornament choice hints at what Ann Michael has planned beyond decorating.

According to Minted, she plays mahjong with other Patriots players’ partners and included personalized mahjong ornaments on the tree.

By the staircase, a sign gives the game its own holiday billing, welcoming guests to “Merry Mahjong,” hosted by Ann Michael Maye.

For that occasion, Ann Michael traded her striped sweater for a sleeveless red dress with a floral scarf tied at the waist.

It has been revealed that she poses beside a dark wood banister draped with evergreen garland. A long spray of greenery falls nearly to the floor at the foot of the stairs, secured with burgundy ribbon that picks up the color of her dress.

The game tables are set beside a lit brick fireplace, where patterned stockings hang from a white mantel topped with greenery and tall red candles.

At the nearest table, wooden tile racks frame a blue-and-white playing mat with a large flower at its center.

A second game is ready to go by the window, and a red drink garnished with a sprig of greenery sits within reach of the first.

Ann Michael carried the personalization right down to the seating. Ribbons fasten little name tags to the backs of the bamboo-style chairs, each fitted with a blue-and-white striped cushion.

According to recent reports, in the final fireside portrait, she takes her place at the tiles. The tag tied behind her reads “Ann Michael.”.

Drake and Ann Michael, both 23, tied the knot in June 2025, having met in middle school in North Carolina. The couple purchased their first home together in Massachusetts in April—and moved in together in July, after Ann Michael graduated from the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, where they both attended college.

Since graduating, Ann Michael has been by her husband's side for almost all of his games, traveling across the U.S. to many of the Patriots' matchups—while also continuing to share insights into her experiences online, earning a legion of followers in the process.

To date, Ann Michael boasts more than 1 million followers across TikTok and Instagram, where she reveals what life is really like as one of the NFL's most popular WAGs—a term that refers to the wives and girlfriends of high-profile athletes.

Ann Michael first rose to social media stardom for her baking skills, which she has heavily documented online.

Drake has admitted that he is not blessed with the same skills as his wife in the kitchen and leaves the baking to her, confessing that the most he can whip up is a "good bacon, egg, and cheese.".

During a press conference, Drake gushed about his wife, noting that he was grateful for her support during his career.

“After we got married, she came up here and had never lived up North. [She] had never seen this much snow on the ground, so obviously it was an adjustment for her," he said.

"She’s loved it, she’s loved the people up here, living up here, [and] she loves the support. She’s got her own little journey that’s been awesome, being herself, and that’s the best thing about her and what I love her for.".

He added, “Her watching my middle school football games playing quarterback to now getting a chance to watch me in the Super Bowl ... I wouldn’t rather do it with anybody else.".

The football star also commented on his decision to marry early, after the couple tied the knot in 2025.

According to recent reports, “My teammates have the right to whatever they choose, but I would definitely advise them to eventually get married. It’s one of the best things I’ve experienced in my life. There’s no better feeling than coming home to a wife that loves you and cares for you.

“I know my teammates, some of them are experiencing different parts of their life. I chose to get married young, and I don’t regret it one bit,” he said.

A little-known protein could be a powerful weapon against Alzheimer’s

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1415 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A protein that helps protect the brain may offer scientists a promising fresh way to fight Alzheimer's disease and other forms of dementia.
  • In a recent development, the findings, published in Science Advances by scientists at Sanford Burnham Prebys, suggest that strengthening the brain's own protective mechanisms could eventually lead to fresh treatments for neurodegenerative diseases.
  • In a recent development, the discovery is particularly significant because tau plays an essential role in keeping healthy brain cells functioning.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A protein that helps protect the brain may offer scientists a promising fresh way to fight Alzheimer's disease and other forms of dementia. Researchers have discovered that increasing levels of this protein can reduce the buildup of toxic tangles associated with brain damage, while also helping preserve the connections that allow nerve cells to communicate.

In a recent development, the findings, published in Science Advances by scientists at Sanford Burnham Prebys, suggest that strengthening the brain's own protective mechanisms could eventually lead to fresh treatments for neurodegenerative diseases. In experiments with mice, the researchers found that boosting the protein reduced several damaging changes associated with Alzheimer's, including brain shrinkage and the accumulation of abnormal tau proteins.

In a recent development, the discovery is particularly significant because tau plays an essential role in keeping healthy brain cells functioning. Under normal conditions, tau proteins help stabilize microtubules, tiny structures that provide internal support to neurons and help maintain the intricate networks of the nervous system.

Sources indicate that in Alzheimer's and several related disorders, however, tau proteins can become abnormal and stick together, forming harmful clumps known as tau tangles. These tangles disrupt the normal functioning of nerve cells and are associated with cognitive decline and neuronal death. Diseases characterized by abnormal tau accumulation are collectively called tauopathies.

A Protective Protein With a Surprising Role in Alzheimer's.

The researchers investigated a protein called sorting-related receptor with A-type repeats (SORLA), which has already attracted scientific attention for its potential role in protecting the brain against Alzheimer's disease.

In a recent development, previous studies have shown that SORLA can help limit the production and accumulation of amyloid-beta, another protein closely associated with Alzheimer's. Amyloid-beta can build up into plaques in the brain, making it one of the disease's major pathological hallmarks alongside tau tangles.

"In the last 15 or 20 years, considerable data has come out from our lab and other groups showing that SORLA can suppress one of the hallmarks of Alzheimer's disease -- amyloid-beta generation and accumulation," said Timothy Huang, PhD, assistant professor in the Center for Neurologic Diseases at Sanford Burnham Prebys.

"Very little was known, however, about whether SORLA affected the tau tangles reflected on the other side of the coin in Alzheimer's disease.".

Sources indicate that to investigate this question, the scientists developed a mouse model by breeding animals engineered to produce additional human SORLA with mice that develop tau tangles, brain atrophy, and cognitive impairments. This allowed them to examine whether higher SORLA levels could reduce tau accumulation and protect against the damage it causes.

Boosting SORLA Reduces Toxic Tau and Brain Shrinkage.

The results revealed that additional SORLA provided protection against several processes that contribute to tau tangles and the progression of neurodegenerative disease.

One important effect involved a process called hyperphosphorylation. This occurs when too many phosphate groups attach to tau proteins, altering their behavior and contributing to the development of harmful tangles. Higher SORLA levels reduced this abnormal modification.

Recent findings suggest that the protein also limited the ability of misfolded tau to act as "seeds" that encourage other tau proteins to clump together. This seeding process can help toxic tau aggregates multiply and spread their damaging effects.

Beyond reducing tau abnormalities, SORLA helped preserve synapses, the specialized connections through which neurons communicate. It also protected synaptic plasticity, the brain's ability to strengthen or modify those connections, which is essential for learning, memory, and normal cognitive function.

"When you upregulate SORLA, you can suppress the negative effects found in tauopathies," mentioned Huijie Huang, PhD, a staff scientist in the Huang lab at Sanford Burnham Prebys and lead author of the study.

"We found there was less brain atrophy and less tau accumulation, which was very exciting to see.".

Removing the Protein Makes Brain Damage Worse.

After observing the benefits of increasing SORLA, the researchers examined what would happen if the protein were missing entirely.

SORLA is produced using instructions encoded by a gene called Sorl1. Some people carry mutations that interfere with this gene's function, potentially disrupting the production or activity of the protective protein.

To investigate the consequences, the team studied genetically modified mice that lacked Sorl1 and therefore could not produce SORLA.

The results contrasted sharply with those seen in mice carrying additional copies of the protein. Instead of protecting against tau-related damage, the absence of SORLA made the harmful effects more severe.

Sources indicate that "The opposite turned out to be true when we deleted the ability to produce SORLA proteins," noted Tim Huang, senior and corresponding author of the manuscript. "A lack of SORLA exacerbated the harmful effects observed in tauopathies.".

These contrasting results provided further evidence that SORLA plays an key protective role in the brain and may influence how severely tau-related diseases progress.

A Upcoming Clue Could Lead to Alzheimer's Treatments.

To understand why changing SORLA levels had such different effects, the researchers examined the molecular activity of individual brain cells and the surrounding tissue.

They combined advanced sequencing methods to measure protein levels and gene activity in individual cells with techniques that map where RNA and proteins are located within brain tissue. This detailed approach helped reveal how SORLA influences the biological processes involved in neurodegeneration.

The analysis indicated that increasing SORLA helped prevent harmful changes in protein production at synapses while also suppressing other mechanisms associated with tauopathy progression.

Industry observers note that the researchers also discovered that higher SORLA levels reduced abnormal gene activity in glial cells. These cells perform several essential functions in the nervous system, including supporting, maintaining, and protecting neurons. Changes in glial cell activity can contribute to the progression of neurodegenerative diseases.

One finding was especially intriguing because it pointed toward a potential target for existing medications.

"One particularly notable finding that we can build on is the upregulation of a member of the plexin-B family of receptors in the absence of SORLA," noted Huijie Huang.

Industry observers note that plexin-B receptors are proteins involved in cellular signaling, helping cells respond to information from their surroundings. The increased activity of a receptor in this family when SORLA was absent suggests that this signaling pathway could be involved in some of the damaging changes associated with tau disorders.

Importantly, drugs capable of targeting this family of receptors already exist, raising the possibility that scientists could investigate whether they might be useful against tau-related dementia.

Sources indicate that "There are unique drugs that can target this class of receptors that we may be able to apply to tau-related dementia disorders," said Tim Huang. "One potential future direction is to repurpose these drugs to target overactivation of glial cells and perhaps reverse some of the phenotypes in tauopathies.".

The Next Step Toward Human Alzheimer's Research.

Although the findings are encouraging, the protective effects were demonstrated in mice, and more research is needed to determine how these mechanisms operate in humans.

According to recent reports, the team now hopes to investigate how individual types of brain cells respond when SORLA levels increase or decrease. One planned approach involves transplanting human neurons or glial cells into mouse brains, allowing researchers to examine the effects of different SORLA mutations in a living brain affected by disease.

"Mouse cells and human cells are different," noted Tim Huang. "Because we're looking at human disease, it's more informative if we can observe the modulation and dysfunction of SORLA in the context of a human cell inside of a diseased brain environment.".

These experiments could help clarify how SORLA protects neurons from toxic tau accumulation and why disruptions in its function make neurodegeneration worse.

It has been revealed that ultimately, the researchers hope that a deeper understanding of this protective protein will reveal new treatment strategies, either by enhancing SORLA's activity or by repurposing existing drugs to interfere with damaging cellular pathways. Such approaches could eventually offer new ways to combat Alzheimer's disease and other forms of dementia driven by toxic tau tangles.

The study was supported by the National Institutes of Health, National Cancer Institute and National Institute on Aging.
